title: PHIL 101: Introduction to Philosophy
subject: Philosophy
description: A question-led introduction to philosophy, focused primarily on the Western tradition. Read primary texts, reconstruct arguments, test objections, and develop your own position. Write and save your work in your own document workspace.
objectives: Identify central questions in metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, religion, and political philosophy.
Reconstruct premises, conclusions, and assumptions in a primary text.
Evaluate reasoning using counterexamples and charitable objections.
Compare competing approaches to a shared philosophical question.
Defend a position in clear prose with passage references, objections, and replies.
studyGuide:
Read once for the question and argument, then return to difficult passages. Primary-reading task estimates include an initial close reading; the separate consolidation task is for rereading, argument maps, and notes. Readings and lecture tasks have distinct outputs. Use a short study session when helpful and record time honestly; a timer is a planning aid, not proof of learning.

At the end of each week, recall one argument without your notes, compare it with the source, and correct it. Record a changed belief or uncertainty in your external learning journal. The study guide includes original argument exercises, model reasoning, and a self-review rubric. Open it from an exercise task.
sourceNotes:
The core text is OpenStax *Introduction to Philosophy*. Public-domain primary texts use the editions linked in each task; pagination and translation vary. Cite section, book, chapter, meditation, or passage identifiers where possible. The Descartes link is Jonathan Bennett's modern-language adaptation at Early Modern Texts, not a historical translation. Crash Course links point to individual official episode pages. All required texts are freely available online; see the access notice above.

This course concentrates on a Western introductory canon. It is a foundation for further study, not a survey of all philosophical traditions. OpenStax provides some comparative context; a subsequent course should give sustained attention to traditions underrepresented here.

title: POLS 101: American Civics, The Federal Government
subject: Political Science
description: An introduction to the United States federal government focusing on how the three branches interlock, their constitutional responsibilities, and the system of checks and balances that binds them. Read the Constitution and Federalist Papers alongside a modern textbook, trace power from founding theory to present-day practice, and develop a working understanding of how legislation becomes law, how the executive enforces it, and how the judiciary interprets it.
objectives: Explain the constitutional design of separation of powers and checks and balances.
Identify the specific powers granted to each branch by Articles I, II, and III.
Trace the legislative process from bill introduction to presidential signature or veto override.
Analyze the presidency as both head of state and head of government, including executive orders, pardons, and treaty power.
Describe the federal court system from district courts to the Supreme Court and the role of judicial review.
Evaluate how interbranch tensions, from impeachment to veto overrides to judicial confirmation, shape policy outcomes.
Assess the role of the federal bureaucracy as the fourth branch and its relationship to all three constitutional branches.
Apply constitutional reasoning to current events involving interbranch conflict.

tasks.title: Crash Course #7: Congressional Committees
tasks.prompt: Watch Crash Course Government #7. Explain why committees are where the real work of Congress happens. Note the difference between standing, select, and joint committees.
tasks.output: One paragraph on why committees are the real engine of Congress.
checklist: Distinguish standing, select, and joint committees.
Explain the role of committee chairs.

tasks.title: Federalist Nos. 62-63: The Senate
tasks.prompt: Read Federalist 62 and 63. Madison (or Hamilton) defends the Senate as a deliberative body that tempers popular passion. Reconstruct the argument for a six-year term with staggered elections. Then evaluate: does the modern Senate still serve this cooling function?
tasks.output: Reconstruction of the Senate's purpose with present-day evaluation.
checklist: Explain the argument for six-year staggered terms.
Identify the cooling saucer metaphor's origin.
Evaluate whether the modern Senate serves this function.

tasks.title: Reading response 5: The filibuster and majority rule
tasks.prompt: In 250-300 words, analyze the filibuster as a check on majority power within the legislative branch itself. Is it consistent with the Framers' design? Consider Madison's argument in Federalist 62 for a deliberative Senate against the practical reality of modern filibuster use.
tasks.output: ~250-300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Define the filibuster and how it works.
Connect it to Madison's vision for the Senate.
Take a position on whether it serves or undermines that vision.

weeklySchedule.topic: The presidency: constitutional design and powers

tasks.title: OpenStax Ch. 12: The Presidency
tasks.prompt: Read the first half of Chapter 12. List the constitutional powers of the president from Article II, separating them into domestic (commander in chief, appointments, pardons) and shared powers (treaties, legislation). Note which powers are checked by other branches.
tasks.output: Two-column list of presidential powers (domestic vs. shared) with checks noted.
checklist: List all Article II powers.
Separate domestic from shared powers.
Note which branch checks each power.

tasks.title: Crash Course #11: Presidential Powers
tasks.prompt: Watch Crash Course Government #11. Note how Benzine distinguishes formal powers (in the Constitution) from informal powers ( precedent and practice). Identify one informal power that has become more important than any formal power.
tasks.output: One paragraph on the most consequential informal presidential power.
tasks.documentName: W06 - Crash Course presidential powers notes
checklist: Distinguish formal from informal powers.
Identify the most consequential informal power with reasoning.

tasks.title: Federalist No. 70: The executive department
tasks.prompt: Read Federalist 70. Hamilton argues for a single executive rather than a plural one. Reconstruct his argument: why is energy in the executive essential, and why does a single person provide it better than a committee? Then identify the danger he acknowledges and how the Constitution guards against it.
tasks.output: Reconstruction of Hamilton's argument with the acknowledged danger and constitutional safeguard.
checklist: Explain why Hamilton wants a single executive.
Define what he means by energy in the executive.
Identify the danger and the safeguard against it.

tasks.title: Reading response 6: Has the presidency grown beyond the Framers' design?
tasks.prompt: In 250-300 words, assess whether the modern presidency exceeds what Hamilton envisioned in Federalist 70. Identify one presidential power that has expanded significantly beyond the original text and explain how that expansion happened (statute, precedent, court ruling, or practice).
tasks.output: ~250-300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Reference Hamilton's argument from Federalist 70.
Identify one specific expanded power.
Explain the mechanism of expansion.

weeklySchedule.topic: The presidency in action: vetoes, orders, and interbranch tension

tasks.title: OpenStax Ch. 12 (second half): The Presidency in Practice
tasks.prompt: Read the second half of Chapter 12. Focus on the veto power, executive orders, signing statements, and the president's role in foreign policy. Trace how each tool creates friction with Congress or the courts.
tasks.output: Notes on each presidential tool and its interbranch friction point.
tasks.documentName: W07 - OpenStax presidency in practice notes
checklist: Explain the veto and how Congress can override it.
Define executive orders and their limits.
Note what signing statements are and the controversy around them.
Identify the president's foreign policy advantages over Congress.

tasks.title: Crash Course #12: Presidential Power and Crises
tasks.prompt: Watch Crash Course Government #12. Note how Benzine frames the expansion of presidential power during crises. Identify one historical crisis that permanently expanded executive power.
tasks.output: One paragraph on a crisis that permanently expanded presidential power.
tasks.documentName: W07 - Crash Course crisis power notes
checklist: Identify a specific historical crisis.
Explain how it expanded executive power permanently.

tasks.title: Federalist No. 75: The treaty-making power
tasks.prompt: Read Federalist 75. Hamilton defends giving the president and Senate shared treaty power rather than giving it to one or the other alone. Reconstruct his argument for this shared arrangement. Then evaluate it against the modern practice of executive agreements, which bypass Senate ratification.
tasks.output: Reconstruction of the shared treaty argument and evaluation against executive agreements.
checklist: Explain why Hamilton wants both president and Senate involved in treaties.
Define executive agreements and how they differ from treaties.
Evaluate whether executive agreements undermine Hamilton's design.

tasks.title: Reading response 7: Veto power as legislative check
tasks.prompt: In 250-300 words, analyze the presidential veto as a legislative check. When is a veto most effective, and when can Congress override it? Use one real example of a veto override and one of a veto that stood. What does the veto threat reveal about executive-legislative negotiation?
tasks.output: ~250-300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Explain when vetoes are most effective.
Provide one override example and one sustained veto.
Analyze the veto threat as a negotiating tool.

weeklySchedule.topic: Midterm: foundations and the first two branches

tasks.title: Study review: consolidate weeks 1-7
tasks.prompt: Review all reading notes from weeks 1-7. Create a one-page study sheet mapping the constitutional design: Article I powers, Article II powers, federalism, and the checks between branches. You will use this sheet during the midterm.
tasks.output: One-page study sheet with constitutional design map.
checklist: Map all three articles to their branches.
List all cross-branch checks.
Include the major Federalist Papers arguments.

tasks.title: Midterm exam (120 minutes)
tasks.prompt: Take a 120-minute self-timed exam covering weeks 1-7. Part 1: Ten short-answer questions on constitutional structure, congressional powers, and presidential powers. Part 2: One essay (choose one of three prompts) analyzing how the legislative and executive branches check each other. Use your study sheet. Write answers in your external workspace.
tasks.output: Completed exam with 10 short answers and 1 essay in your external workspace.
checklist: Answer all 10 short-answer questions.
Write one complete essay with a thesis and evidence.
Time yourself honestly at 120 minutes.

tasks.title: Midterm self-review
tasks.prompt: After completing the midterm, review your answers honestly. Identify two topics you understood well and two you need to revisit before the final. Write a brief plan for how you will strengthen the weak areas in the second half of the course.
tasks.output: Self-review with two strengths, two weaknesses, and a improvement plan.
checklist: Identify two strong topics.
Identify two weak topics.
Write a concrete plan to improve each weak area.

weeklySchedule.topic: The federal courts: structure and jurisdiction

tasks.title: OpenStax Ch. 13: The Courts
tasks.prompt: Read the first half of Chapter 13. Map the three tiers of the federal court system: district courts, circuit courts, and the Supreme Court. Explain how cases move between tiers and what each tier does. Note the difference between original jurisdiction and appellate jurisdiction.
tasks.output: Diagram or map of the federal court system with jurisdictions noted.
checklist: Map all three tiers with their roles.
Distinguish original from appellate jurisdiction.
Explain how a case reaches the Supreme Court (certiorari).

tasks.title: Crash Course #21: Structure of the Court System
tasks.prompt: Watch Crash Course Government #21. Note how Benzine explains the dual court system (state and federal). Identify one situation where a case could be heard in either system and explain what determines where it goes.
tasks.output: One paragraph on concurrent jurisdiction and forum selection.
tasks.documentName: W09 - Crash Course court structure notes
checklist: Explain the dual court system.
Identify when state and federal courts overlap.
Note what determines which court hears a case.

tasks.title: Article III of the Constitution, with annotation
tasks.prompt: Read Article III using the Constitution Annotated. Note that Article III is remarkably short. List what it does establish (supreme Court, inferior courts as Congress creates them, lifetime tenure, salary protection) and what it leaves to Congress. Why did the Framers leave so much unspecified?
tasks.output: List of what Article III establishes and what it leaves to Congress.
checklist: List what Article III explicitly establishes.
Identify at least three things left to Congress.
Explain why lifetime tenure matters for judicial independence.

tasks.title: Reading response 9: Judicial independence and democratic accountability
tasks.prompt: In 250-300 words, analyze the tension between judicial independence (lifetime tenure, salary protection) and democratic accountability. Should federal judges be completely insulated from public opinion, or does that create a democratic deficit? Reference Article III's design choices.
tasks.output: ~250-300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Reference Article III's tenure and salary provisions.
Identify the democratic deficit argument.
Take and defend a position.

weeklySchedule.topic: Judicial review, the Supreme Court, and constitutional interpretation

tasks.title: OpenStax Ch. 13 (second half): The Supreme Court and Judicial Review
tasks.prompt: Read the second half of Chapter 13. Focus on judicial review, the power to declare acts of Congress or the president unconstitutional. Trace how Marbury v. Madison established this power. Note how the Court checks both other branches and how both other branches check the Court.
tasks.output: Notes on judicial review's origin and all checks between the Court and other branches.
checklist: Explain Marbury v. Madison and its significance.
List checks the Court has on Congress and the president.
List checks Congress and the president have on the Court.

tasks.title: Crash Course #22: Supreme Court of the United States
tasks.prompt: Watch Crash Course Government #22. Note how Benzine explains the nomination and confirmation process. Identify the political factors that shape who gets nominated and how the Senate's role has changed over time.
tasks.output: One paragraph on how nomination politics has changed.
tasks.documentName: W10 - Crash Course Supreme Court notes
checklist: Explain the nomination and confirmation process.
Identify political factors in nomination choices.
Note how the Senate's role has evolved.

tasks.title: Federalist No. 78: The judiciary department
tasks.prompt: Read Federalist 78 carefully. Hamilton calls the judiciary the least dangerous branch. Reconstruct his argument for why. Then identify the specific power he discusses that makes the judiciary powerful despite having no sword or purse. Evaluate: was Hamilton right that the judiciary is the least dangerous branch?
tasks.output: Reconstruction of the least dangerous branch argument with evaluation.
checklist: Explain why Hamilton calls the judiciary least dangerous.
Identify the specific power that makes it powerful (judicial review).
Evaluate whether the claim holds up today.

tasks.title: Branch analysis paper 1: The judiciary as constitutional referee
tasks.prompt: Write a 4-5 page paper (approximately 1200-1500 words) analyzing the judiciary's role as the referee of constitutional disputes between the other two branches. Use Federalist 78, Marbury v. Madison, and at least one modern Supreme Court case where the Court ruled on a separation-of-powers dispute. Address: What gives the Court authority to rule on interbranch conflicts? What happens when the other branches resist?
tasks.output: 4-5 page paper in your external workspace.
checklist: Reference Federalist 78 and Marbury v. Madison.
Analyze at least one modern separation-of-powers case.
Address what happens when branches resist Court rulings.
Include a clear thesis and conclusion.

weeklySchedule.topic: The federal bureaucracy: the fourth branch?

tasks.title: OpenStax Ch. 15: The Bureaucracy
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 15. Explain how the bureaucracy implements laws passed by Congress and directives from the president. Note how Congress, the president, and the courts each check the bureaucracy. Identify the iron triangle (agencies, committees, interest groups) and how it creates stability in policy.
tasks.output: Notes on bureaucratic function, interbranch checks on agencies, and the iron triangle.
checklist: Explain how the bureaucracy implements laws.
List checks from each branch on the bureaucracy.
Define the iron triangle and its components.

tasks.title: Crash Course #28: The Bureaucracy
tasks.prompt: Watch Crash Course Government #28. Note how Benzine frames the tension between bureaucratic expertise and democratic accountability. Is it a problem that unelected civil servants make consequential policy decisions?
tasks.output: One paragraph on the expertise vs. accountability tension.
checklist: Identify the expertise argument for bureaucracy.
Identify the accountability concern.
State your view on whether the tension is resolvable.

tasks.title: Article II, Section 3: The Take Care Clause
tasks.prompt: Read Article II, Section 3 using the Constitution Annotated. Focus on the Take Care Clause (the president must take care that the laws be faithfully executed). Explain how this clause connects the president to the bureaucracy. How does it create both presidential power over agencies and a duty to implement laws Congress passes?
tasks.output: Notes on the Take Care Clause and its dual function.
checklist: Quote the Take Care Clause.
Explain how it gives the president power over agencies.
Explain how it creates a duty to implement congressional law.

tasks.title: Reading response 11: Is the bureaucracy a fourth branch?
tasks.prompt: In 250-300 words, evaluate the claim that the federal bureaucracy has become a de facto fourth branch of government. What gives agencies quasi-legislative (rulemaking) and quasi-judicial (adjudication) powers? Is this consistent with the constitutional design, or a necessary adaptation?
tasks.output: ~250-300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Define quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial powers.
Take a position on whether the bureaucracy is a fourth branch.
Connect your argument to the constitutional design.

weeklySchedule.topic: Checks and balances in action: impeachment, confirmation, and oversight

tasks.title: OpenStax review: impeachment and oversight
tasks.prompt: Review the impeachment sections of OpenStax Chapters 11 and 12. Trace the full impeachment process: House impeachment, Senate trial, chief justice presiding, two-thirds vote. Then identify Congress's oversight tools (hearings, subpoenas, Government Accountability Office, inspector generals). How do these checks work in practice vs. theory?
tasks.output: Notes on impeachment process and congressional oversight tools.
checklist: Map the full impeachment process step by step.
List at least four oversight tools Congress uses.
Note one gap between theory and practice in oversight.

tasks.title: Crash Course #9 and #10: Congressional and Presidential oversight
tasks.prompt: Watch Crash Course Government episodes on congressional oversight and the presidency's relationship with Congress. Note one real example where congressional oversight changed executive branch behavior.
tasks.output: One paragraph on a real oversight example that changed executive behavior.
checklist: Identify a specific oversight example.
Explain how it changed executive branch behavior.

tasks.title: Constitution: impeachment clauses in Articles I and II
tasks.prompt: Read the impeachment clauses using the Constitution Annotated: Article I, Section 2 (House power to impeach), Article I, Section 3 (Senate power to try, two-thirds vote), Article II, Section 4 (grounds: treason, bribery, high crimes and misdemeanors). Explain what high crimes and misdemeanors means and why the Framers left it vague.
tasks.output: Notes on each impeachment clause with analysis of the high crimes standard.
checklist: List each constitutional impeachment clause.
Explain the high crimes and misdemeanors standard.
Note why the Framers left it undefined.

tasks.title: Branch analysis paper 2: When checks collide
tasks.prompt: Write a 4-5 page paper (approximately 1200-1500 words) analyzing a historical or recent episode where two or more branches clashed over constitutional authority. Options include: a Supreme Court nomination fight, an impeachment, a presidential veto override, a court ruling against an executive order, or a congressional subpoena dispute. Address: What constitutional provisions were invoked? Which branch won? Did the system work as designed?
tasks.output: 4-5 page paper in your external workspace.
tasks.documentName: W12 - Branch analysis 2 - When checks collide
checklist: Choose a specific interbranch conflict.
Identify the constitutional provisions invoked by each side.
Explain the outcome and whether the system worked as designed.
Include a thesis and conclusion.

weeklySchedule.topic: Civil liberties and civil rights: how all three branches protect and restrict rights

tasks.title: OpenStax Ch. 4 and 5: Civil Liberties and Civil Rights
tasks.prompt: Read Chapters 4 and 5 (skim the detail, focus on structure). Identify how each branch is involved in rights protection: Congress passes civil rights legislation, the executive enforces it, and the courts interpret it. Trace one right through all three branches to show the interlock.
tasks.output: Notes tracing one right through all three branches.
tasks.documentName: W13 - Civil liberties and rights notes
checklist: Trace one right through Congress, president, and courts.
Note where the branches agree and where they conflict.
Identify the role of the 14th Amendment in rights enforcement.

tasks.title: Crash Course #23-24: Civil Liberties and Civil Rights
tasks.prompt: Watch Crash Course Government episodes on civil liberties and civil rights. Note how Benzine distinguishes liberties (protections from government) from rights (guarantees of equal treatment). How does this distinction map onto the three branches' roles?
tasks.output: One paragraph distinguishing liberties from rights through the lens of the three branches.
checklist: Distinguish civil liberties from civil rights.
Map each to the branch most responsible for enforcing it.

tasks.title: Bill of Rights and Reconstruction Amendments
tasks.prompt: Read the Bill of Rights (Amendments 1-10) and the Reconstruction Amendments (13, 14, 15) using the Constitution Annotated. Focus on how the 14th Amendment's Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses became the primary tool for the federal judiciary to check state governments on rights issues.
tasks.output: Notes on the 14th Amendment's role in federal rights enforcement.
checklist: List the key clauses of the 14th Amendment.
Explain how Due Process applies the Bill of Rights to states (incorporation).
Explain how Equal Protection checks state discrimination.

tasks.title: Reading response 13: All three branches and one right
tasks.prompt: In 250-300 words, trace one specific right (e.g., freedom of speech, equal protection, due process) through all three branches. Show what Congress did (legislation), what the president did (enforcement), and what the courts did (interpretation). Where did the branches conflict, and how was it resolved?
tasks.output: ~250-300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Choose one specific right.
Show action from each of the three branches.
Identify where they conflicted and how it was resolved.

weeklySchedule.topic: Final paper: research, outline, and draft

tasks.title: Final paper proposal
tasks.prompt: Write a 1-page proposal for your final paper. Choose a topic that analyzes how the three branches interlock around a single issue. Examples: how a bill becomes law through all three branches, how national security power is shared and contested, how a major policy change required action from all three branches. State your thesis, the constitutional provisions you will analyze, and the sources you plan to use.
tasks.output: 1-page proposal with thesis, constitutional provisions, and source list.
checklist: State a clear thesis about interbranch interaction.
List the constitutional provisions you will analyze.
Identify at least three sources beyond the textbook.

tasks.title: Final paper: source notes and research
tasks.prompt: Gather and annotate your sources. For each source, write a 2-3 sentence note on what it contributes to your argument. Include at least: the Constitution (relevant articles/clauses), two Federalist Papers, one Supreme Court case, and two secondary sources (news articles, academic articles, or C-SPAN resources).
tasks.output: Annotated source list with at least 6 sources.
checklist: Include the Constitution with specific clauses.
Include at least two Federalist Papers.
Include at least one Supreme Court case.
Write 2-3 sentences on each source's contribution.

tasks.title: Final paper: outline
tasks.prompt: Write a detailed outline for your final paper (8-10 pages, approximately 2500-3000 words). Include: introduction with thesis, one section per branch showing its role, a section on how the branches interact, and a conclusion that evaluates whether the system worked as the Framers intended. Under each section, list the evidence and sources you will use.
tasks.output: Detailed outline with evidence mapped to each section.
checklist: Include thesis in the introduction.
Devote one section to each branch's role.
Include an interaction section.
Map evidence and sources under each section.

tasks.title: Final paper: first draft
tasks.prompt: Write the first full draft of your final paper following your outline. Aim for 2500-3000 words. Do not polish yet. Focus on getting the argument complete: each branch's role, the interaction, and the evaluation. Cite all sources as you go.
tasks.output: Complete first draft (2500-3000 words) in your external workspace.
checklist: Write 2500-3000 words.
Cover all three branches plus interaction.
Cite sources as you write.
End with a conclusion that evaluates the Framers' design.

weeklySchedule.topic: Final paper revision and course reflection

tasks.title: Final paper: revision
tasks.prompt: Revise your final paper draft. Focus on: strengthening the thesis, ensuring each branch section has specific constitutional evidence, tightening the interaction analysis, and clarifying the conclusion. Check that every claim has a source. Read the paper aloud to catch awkward passages.
tasks.output: Revised final paper (2500-3000 words) in your external workspace.
checklist: Thesis is specific and arguable.
Each branch section has constitutional evidence.
Every claim has a source.
Conclusion evaluates the Framers' design.

tasks.title: Final paper: self-review
tasks.prompt: After revising, write a 1-page self-review. Identify the strongest part of your paper and the weakest. Note one argument you wish you had more space to develop. Rate your confidence in your understanding of how the three branches interlock on a scale of 1-5 and explain why.
tasks.output: 1-page self-review with strengths, weaknesses, and confidence rating.
checklist: Identify the strongest section.
Identify the weakest section.
Rate confidence 1-5 with explanation.

tasks.title: Course reflection: how the branches interlock
tasks.prompt: Write a 2-3 page reflection on what you learned about the federal government. Address: How did your understanding of checks and balances change? Which branch do you now think is most powerful, and why? What surprised you most about how the branches interact? What would you study next?
tasks.output: 2-3 page reflection in your external workspace.
checklist: Describe how your understanding of checks and balances evolved.
Identify the most powerful branch with reasoning.
Note the most surprising thing you learned.
Suggest a next topic to study.

tasks.title: Export progress and save final work
tasks.prompt: Export your Syllabi progress from the Settings page. Save the JSON file to your 06 Reflection and Progress/Progress Exports folder. Verify all task statuses are marked complete. Save a final copy of your final paper and reflection in your course folder.
tasks.output: Exported progress JSON and verified completion record.
checklist: Export the progress JSON from Settings.
Verify all tasks are marked complete.
Save final paper and reflection in the course folder.

title: ECON 301: Game Theory and Strategic Analysis
subject: Economics
description: An intermediate introduction to game theory covering static and dynamic games with complete and incomplete information. Learn to model strategic interactions, compute Nash equilibria, analyze sequential games with backward induction, and apply game-theoretic reasoning to economics, politics, and everyday life. Combines formal theory with real-world applications.
objectives: Model strategic situations using normal form and extensive form game representations.
Identify and compute Nash equilibria in pure and mixed strategies.
Apply backward induction and subgame perfect equilibrium to sequential games.
Analyze games of incomplete information using Bayesian Nash equilibrium and perfect Bayesian equilibrium.
Evaluate repeated games, bargaining problems, and auction mechanisms.
Apply cooperative game theory concepts including the Shapley value and the core.
Critically assess the assumptions of rationality and common knowledge in game-theoretic models.

resources.label: Yale Open Courses: Game Theory (Ben Polak, ECON 159)
resources.note: 23 free video lectures from Yale's introductory game theory course. Core video resource for the course.

resources.label: Osborne & Rubinstein, A Course in Game Theory
resources.note: Free full-text PDF. Graduate-level reference for proofs and formal definitions. Use as supplementary reference.

resources.label: Tadelis, Game Theory: An Introduction (Princeton, 2013)
resources.note: Primary textbook. Advanced undergraduate level. Covers static and dynamic games, incomplete information, auctions, mechanism design, signaling.

resources.label: Game Theory 101 (William Spaniel)
resources.note: Free video lectures and textbook. Covers strict dominance through perfect Bayesian equilibrium. Excellent supplementary resource with worked examples.

resources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Game Theory
resources.note: Philosophical foundations and interpretations. Required reading for conceptual understanding.

resources.label: Ben Polak Game Theory Lectures (YouTube Playlist)
resources.note: YouTube version of the Yale Open Courses lectures. Same content as yale-polak, use either platform.

folderStructure: 00 Course Guide/Learning Goals and Study Plan

weeklySchedule.topic: Introduction to Strategic Thinking

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 1-2: Introduction and Rational Choice
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapters 1-2. Take notes on the definition of rationality, the concept of utility, and how strategic situations differ from parametric decision problems. Write down one real-world example of a strategic situation you encountered this week.
tasks.output: Notes defining rationality, utility, and strategic vs parametric decisions, plus one personal example.
tasks.documentName: W01 - Tadelis intro and rational choice
checklist: Define rationality in your own words.
Explain the difference between parametric and strategic decisions.
Identify the components of a game: players, actions, payoffs.

tasks.title: Polak Lecture 1: Five First Lessons
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lecture 1. Polak introduces five key lessons through classroom games. Note each lesson and the game that illustrates it. Pay attention to the penalty kick and prisoner's dilemma examples.
tasks.output: List of the five first lessons with the game example for each.
checklist: List all five lessons.
For each lesson, name the game that illustrated it.
Note one insight that surprised you.

tasks.title: Practice: Game matrices and payoff functions
tasks.prompt: Work through Tadelis end-of-chapter exercises for Chapters 1-2. Practice representing simple 2x2 games in normal form. Draw payoff matrices for: Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes, Matching Pennies, and Stag Hunt. For each, label the players, strategies, and payoffs.
tasks.output: Four game matrices with full labeling, plus solutions to assigned exercises.
checklist: All four matrices are correctly drawn.
Payoffs are correctly placed for each player.
Each game is identified by name with a one-line description.

tasks.title: Response: Strategic thinking in the wild
tasks.prompt: Find a news article or real-world scenario involving strategic interaction (business competition, political negotiations, sports). In ~400 words, identify the players, their strategies, and their likely payoffs. Represent the situation as a 2x2 game matrix and predict what you think will happen.
tasks.output: ~400 word analysis with a game matrix and prediction.
checklist: Players and strategies are clearly identified.
Payoff matrix is drawn and labeled.
Prediction is justified by reasoning about the game.

weeklySchedule.topic: Normal Form Games and Dominance

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 3-4: Games in Normal Form and Dominance
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapters 3-4. Focus on: normal form representation, strictly dominated strategies, weakly dominated strategies, and iterated elimination of dominated strategies. Work through every example in the text.
tasks.output: Notes on dominance concepts with definitions in your own words and worked examples.
checklist: Define strict vs weak dominance with an example of each.
Explain iterated elimination and when it is valid.
Note one limitation of dominance as a solution concept.

tasks.title: Polak Lectures 2-3: Empathy and Iterative Deletion
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lectures 2 and 3. Lecture 2 covers putting yourself in others' shoes. Lecture 3 covers iterative deletion of dominated strategies and the median-voter theorem. Take detailed notes on the median-voter application.
tasks.output: Notes on empathetic reasoning, iterative deletion process, and the median-voter theorem model.
checklist: Explain why empathy matters in game theory.
Walk through the iterative deletion process for the location game.
State the median-voter theorem and its assumptions.

tasks.title: Practice: Iterated elimination and dominance
tasks.prompt: Solve 5 games using iterated elimination of dominated strategies. For each game: (1) write the payoff matrix, (2) identify dominated strategies, (3) eliminate iteratively, (4) state the surviving outcome. Use problems from Tadelis exercises and Game Theory 101 practice problems.
tasks.output: 5 solved games with full elimination steps shown.
checklist: Each elimination step is justified.
Final surviving strategies are clearly identified.
Note which games have unique vs multiple solutions.

tasks.title: Response: When dominance fails
tasks.prompt: In ~400 words, explain a situation where iterated elimination of dominated strategies does not yield a unique solution. Construct a 3x3 game matrix where no strategy is dominated. Discuss what this means for the predictive power of dominance as a solution concept.
tasks.output: ~400 word analysis with a constructed 3x3 game matrix and discussion.
checklist: The 3x3 game has no dominated strategies.
The discussion addresses limitations of dominance.
At least one alternative solution concept is mentioned.

weeklySchedule.topic: Nash Equilibrium in Pure Strategies

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 5-6: Nash Equilibrium
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapters 5-6. Focus on the definition of Nash equilibrium, best response functions, and how to find pure strategy Nash equilibria. Work through the Cournot duopoly and Bertrand competition examples carefully.
tasks.output: Notes on Nash equilibrium definition, best response analysis, and Cournot/Bertrand models.
checklist: Define Nash equilibrium precisely in your own words.
Draw best response functions for Cournot duopoly.
Compare Cournot vs Bertrand outcomes.

tasks.title: Polak Lecture 4: Best Responses in Soccer and Business
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lecture 4. Focus on how best responses work in the partnership game. Note how to compute best responses when payoffs are continuous. Try to solve the partnership game before Polak reveals the answer.
tasks.output: Notes on best response functions and the partnership game solution.
checklist: Derive the best response function for each player.
Identify the Nash equilibrium of the partnership game.
Note how continuous strategies change the analysis.

tasks.title: Practice: Finding Nash equilibria
tasks.prompt: Find all pure strategy Nash equilibria in 8 games. Include: Coordination game, Battle of the Sexes, Chicken, Stag Hunt, Cournot duopoly (with specific demand and cost functions), Bertrand duopoly, a 3-player game, and a game with no pure strategy Nash equilibrium. For each, show the best response analysis.
tasks.output: 8 solved games with best response analysis and identified equilibria.
checklist: Best responses are computed for each player.
All Nash equilibria are identified (not just one).
Games with no pure strategy equilibrium are noted.

tasks.title: Response: The meaning of Nash equilibrium
tasks.prompt: Read the SEP entry on Game Theory, sections on Nash equilibrium. In ~500 words, address: What does it mean for a strategy profile to be a Nash equilibrium? Is it a positive prediction, a normative recommendation, or both? Discuss the common knowledge assumptions required.
tasks.output: ~500 word philosophical analysis of Nash equilibrium interpretation.
checklist: Positive vs normative interpretation is addressed.
Common knowledge assumptions are discussed.
At least one critique of Nash equilibrium is presented.

weeklySchedule.topic: Mixed Strategy Nash Equilibrium

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 7: Mixed Strategies
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapter 7 on mixed strategy Nash equilibrium. Focus on: expected utility, indifference principle, how to compute mixed equilibria. Work through the Matching Pennies and Battle of the Sexes examples with mixed strategies.
tasks.output: Notes on mixed strategies, the indifference principle, and worked mixed equilibrium calculations.
checklist: Explain the indifference principle.
Show the calculation for a mixed equilibrium step by step.
Note when mixed equilibria exist vs pure only.

tasks.title: Polak Lectures 5-6: Mixed Strategies in Theory and Practice
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lectures 5 and 6. Lecture 5 covers mixed strategies in the penalty kick game and tennis. Lecture 6 covers mixed strategies in office hours and the volunteer's dilemma. Note how mixed strategies appear in real sports data.
tasks.output: Notes on mixed strategy examples from sports and the volunteer's dilemma.
checklist: Compute the mixed equilibrium for the penalty kick game.
Note the empirical evidence from tennis/soccer data.
Explain the volunteer's dilemma and its mixed solution.

tasks.title: Practice: Computing mixed strategy equilibria
tasks.prompt: Compute all Nash equilibria (pure and mixed) for 6 games: Matching Pennies, Battle of the Sexes, Chicken, Rock-Paper-Scissors, a 3x2 game, and a 2x3 game. For each mixed equilibrium, show: (1) the indifference equations, (2) solving for probabilities, (3) verification that neither player can profitably deviate.
tasks.output: 6 solved games with complete mixed equilibrium calculations and verification.
checklist: Indifference equations are set up correctly.
Probabilities are between 0 and 1.
Each equilibrium is verified by checking for profitable deviations.

tasks.title: Response: Interpreting mixed strategies
tasks.prompt: In ~500 words, address the critique that mixed strategies are unrealistic. Do people actually randomize? Discuss the Harsanyi purification theorem and the alternative interpretation of mixed strategies as beliefs about others' actions. Which interpretation do you find more compelling?
tasks.output: ~500 word essay on the interpretation of mixed strategies.
checklist: The randomization critique is stated fairly.
Harsanyi purification is explained.
Your preferred interpretation is defended with reasoning.

weeklySchedule.topic: Extensive Form Games and Backward Induction

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 8-9: Extensive Form Games
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapters 8-9. Focus on: game trees, information sets, backward induction, and the difference between perfect and imperfect information. Draw game trees for: the entry game, the centipede game, and Stackelberg competition.
tasks.output: Notes on extensive form representation and backward induction with three drawn game trees.
checklist: Game trees are drawn with proper nodes, branches, and payoffs.
Information sets are correctly indicated.
Backward induction steps are shown for each game.

tasks.title: Polak Lecture 7: Backward Induction
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lecture 7 on backward induction. Focus on the commitment problem and how moving first can be advantageous. Note the Stackelberg vs Cournot comparison and the centipede game.
tasks.output: Notes on backward induction, commitment, and first-mover advantage.
checklist: Explain first-mover advantage with an example.
Show backward induction in the Stackelberg game.
Note the tension between backward induction and cooperation in the centipede game.

tasks.title: Practice: Solving extensive form games
tasks.prompt: Solve 5 extensive form games using backward induction: (1) Stackelberg duopoly, (2) a 3-stage bargaining game, (3) the centipede game (3-stage), (4) an entry-deterrence game, (5) a sequential Prisoner's Dilemma. For each, draw the tree and show the backward induction solution.
tasks.output: 5 solved game trees with backward induction paths marked.
checklist: Game trees are correctly drawn.
Backward induction proceeds from terminal nodes.
The equilibrium path is identified in each game.

tasks.title: Response: The centipede game paradox
tasks.prompt: In ~500 words, analyze the centipede game. Backward induction predicts immediate defection, but experimental subjects often cooperate for several rounds. Discuss: (1) Is backward induction rational? (2) What assumptions might be wrong? (3) What does this tell us about the limits of game theory?
tasks.output: ~500 word analysis of the centipede game and backward induction paradox.
checklist: The backward induction solution is correctly stated.
At least two explanations for experimental results are discussed.
The analysis addresses what assumptions might be violated.

weeklySchedule.topic: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 10: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapter 10 on subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE). Focus on: the definition of a subgame, why Nash equilibrium is insufficient for dynamic games, non-credible threats, and the one-shot deviation principle. Work through all examples.
tasks.output: Notes on SPE, non-credible threats, and the one-shot deviation principle.
checklist: Define subgame and subgame perfect equilibrium.
Explain non-credible threats with an example.
State the one-shot deviation principle.

tasks.title: Polak Lectures 8-9: Backward Induction and Reputation
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lectures 8 and 9. Lecture 8 covers backward induction in the joint venture game. Lecture 9 covers reputation and credible commitment. Note how commitment devices change the game structure.
tasks.output: Notes on joint venture analysis and reputation/commitment mechanisms.
checklist: Show the SPE of the joint venture game.
Explain how commitment devices work.
Note the difference between Nash and SPE in these games.

tasks.title: Practice: Subgame perfect equilibrium
tasks.prompt: Find all Nash equilibria and then identify which are subgame perfect for 5 games. Include: a sequential bargaining game (3 periods), an entry game with capacity commitment, a moral hazard in teams game, a legislative veto game, and a multi-stage investment game. Eliminate non-credible threats.
tasks.output: 5 games with all NE identified, then SPE separated from non-credible NE.
checklist: All Nash equilibria are found first.
Non-credible threats are identified and eliminated.
SPE is verified using the one-shot deviation principle.

tasks.title: Midterm self-assessment
tasks.prompt: Write a ~500 word self-assessment of your understanding so far. For each topic (dominance, Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, backward induction, SPE), rate your confidence 1-5 and explain why. Identify the two concepts you most need to review and create a specific plan to strengthen them before the midterm.
tasks.output: ~500 word self-assessment with confidence ratings and review plan.
checklist: Each topic has a confidence rating and explanation.
Two review areas are identified.
The review plan is specific with actions and timing.

weeklySchedule.topic: Repeated Games

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 11: Repeated Games
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapter 11 on repeated games. Focus on: finitely vs infinitely repeated games, the folk theorem, trigger strategies, and tit-for-tat. Understand why cooperation can be sustained in infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma but not in finitely repeated ones.
tasks.output: Notes on repeated games, the folk theorem, trigger strategies, and cooperation conditions.
checklist: Explain why finite repetition fails to sustain cooperation.
State the folk theorem (informal version).
Define trigger strategy and tit-for-tat.

tasks.title: Polak Lectures 10-11: Repeated Interaction
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lectures 10 and 11 on repeated interaction. Focus on the prisoner's dilemma repeated and how cooperative outcomes emerge. Note the comparison between finite and infinite horizon models.
tasks.output: Notes on repeated PD, cooperation under infinite horizon, and real-world applications.
checklist: Show why backward induction fails for infinite games.
Compute the conditions under which cooperation is an equilibrium.
Note at least two real-world applications of repeated games.

tasks.title: Practice: Repeated game analysis
tasks.prompt: Solve 4 repeated game problems: (1) Find the minimum discount factor for cooperation in infinitely repeated PD with grim trigger. (2) Compare grim trigger vs tit-for-tat. (3) Analyze a finitely repeated game (T periods) and show defection is inevitable. (4) For a repeated Cournot game, find conditions for collusion.
tasks.output: 4 solved repeated game problems with discount factor calculations.
checklist: Discount factor conditions are computed correctly.
Grim trigger and tit-for-tat are compared.
The finite case is shown to collapse to defection.

tasks.title: Response: Cooperation and the shadow of the future
tasks.prompt: In ~500 words, apply repeated game theory to a real-world setting: oligopoly collusion, international trade agreements, or environmental cooperation. Identify the game being repeated, the discount factor (or its real-world proxy), and whether cooperation is sustainable. Discuss what factors might destabilize cooperation.
tasks.output: ~500 word applied analysis of cooperation in a real-world repeated game.
checklist: The real-world game is modeled formally.
The discount factor proxy is identified.
At least one destabilizing factor is discussed.

weeklySchedule.topic: Bargaining Theory

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 12: Bargaining
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapter 12 on bargaining. Focus on: the Rubinstein alternating offers model, the relationship between discount factors and bargaining power, and the Nash bargaining solution. Work through the 2-period and 3-period cases explicitly.
tasks.output: Notes on Rubinstein bargaining, discount factors, and Nash bargaining solution.
checklist: Solve the 2-period bargaining game by backward induction.
Explain how discount factors determine bargaining power.
State the Nash bargaining solution axioms.

tasks.title: Polak Lecture 12: Bargaining
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lecture 12 on bargaining. Note how the alternating offers model works and how patience translates into bargaining power. Pay attention to the comparison between cooperative and non-cooperative approaches to bargaining.
tasks.output: Notes on the alternating offers model and the role of patience in bargaining.
checklist: The alternating offers procedure is described.
Patience and bargaining power are connected.
Cooperative vs non-cooperative bargaining is contrasted.

tasks.title: Practice: Bargaining problems
tasks.prompt: Solve 5 bargaining problems: (1) 2-period alternating offers with equal discount factors. (2) 3-period case with unequal discount factors. (3) Infinite horizon Rubinstein model. (4) Nash bargaining solution for a specific disagreement point. (5) A legislative bargaining problem (divide the dollar among 3 players with majority rule).
tasks.output: 5 solved bargaining problems with full backward induction calculations.
checklist: Backward induction is applied correctly in finite cases.
The infinite horizon formula is derived.
The Nash bargaining solution is computed from the disagreement point.

tasks.title: Response: Midterm review synthesis
tasks.prompt: Write a ~600 word synthesis of the first half of the course. Trace the logical progression from dominance to Nash equilibrium to mixed strategies to backward induction to SPE to repeated games to bargaining. For each concept, identify the key limitation that motivated the next concept. This is your midterm preparation document.
tasks.output: ~600 word concept map tracing the logical chain of solution concepts.
checklist: Each concept is linked to the next with its motivating limitation.
All 7 core concepts are covered.
The synthesis reads as a coherent narrative, not a list.

weeklySchedule.topic: Bayesian Games

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 13-14: Bayesian Games
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapters 13-14 on games of incomplete information. Focus on: Harsanyi's framework, types and beliefs, Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE). Work through the Cournot model with unknown costs and the entry game with incomplete information.
tasks.output: Notes on the Harsanyi framework, types, beliefs, and BNE with worked examples.
checklist: Define type, belief, and Bayesian Nash equilibrium.
Show the Cournot model with unknown costs.
Explain the common prior assumption.

tasks.title: Polak Lecture 13: Sequential Bargaining with Incomplete Info
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lecture 13. Focus on how incomplete information changes bargaining outcomes. Note how beliefs update through observed offers and how this connects to the Bayesian framework.
tasks.output: Notes on bargaining with incomplete information and belief updating.
checklist: Explain how incomplete information changes bargaining.
Note how offers signal information.
Connect to the Bayesian Nash equilibrium concept.

tasks.title: Practice: Bayesian Nash equilibrium
tasks.prompt: Solve 4 Bayesian games: (1) Entry game where incumbent's cost is unknown (high or low type). (2) Cournot duopoly where firm 2's marginal cost is unknown. (3) A first-price auction with 2 bidders and uniform valuations. (4) A voting game where voters have private preferences. For each, set up the Bayesian game and find the BNE.
tasks.output: 4 solved Bayesian games with type spaces, beliefs, and BNE strategies.
checklist: Type spaces and prior beliefs are specified.
Each type's best response is computed.
The BNE is verified for each type.

tasks.title: Response: Modeling incomplete information
tasks.prompt: In ~500 words, model a real-world situation with incomplete information as a Bayesian game. Good candidates: job market screening, insurance markets, negotiations with hidden information. Specify players, types, priors, actions, and payoffs. Solve for the BNE or explain why it is difficult to solve.
tasks.output: ~500 word Bayesian game model of a real-world scenario.
checklist: The model has well-defined types and priors.
The payoff structure is specified.
The BNE is solved or the difficulty is explained.

weeklySchedule.topic: Auctions

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 15: Auctions
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapter 15 on auctions. Focus on: the four main auction formats (English, Dutch, first-price sealed-bid, second-price sealed-bid/Vickrey), the revenue equivalence theorem, and optimal auctions. Understand why Vickrey auctions are truth-revealing.
tasks.output: Notes on auction formats, revenue equivalence, and the Vickrey truth-revelation result.
checklist: Compare the four auction formats with a table.
State the revenue equivalence theorem and its assumptions.
Explain why truthful bidding is optimal in a Vickrey auction.

tasks.title: Polak Lecture 14: Auctions
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lecture 14 on auctions. Focus on the different auction formats and how bidders should behave in each. Note the connection between auction theory and real-world auction design (spectrum auctions, art auctions).
tasks.output: Notes on auction formats, bidding behavior, and real-world auction design.
checklist: Bidding strategies for each format are noted.
Revenue equivalence is discussed.
At least one real-world auction design example is included.

tasks.title: Practice: Auction theory problems
tasks.prompt: Solve 5 auction problems: (1) Find the symmetric BNE of a first-price auction with uniform valuations on [0,1]. (2) Show truthful bidding is optimal in a Vickrey auction. (3) Compare expected revenue in first-price vs second-price auctions with uniform values. (4) Analyze an all-pay auction. (5) Consider a common value auction and the winner's curse.
tasks.output: 5 solved auction problems with equilibrium bidding strategies.
checklist: Bidding functions are derived, not just stated.
Revenue equivalence is verified numerically.
The winner's curse is explained in the common value case.

tasks.title: Response: Auction design in practice
tasks.prompt: In ~500 words, analyze a real-world auction: FCC spectrum auctions, Google ad auctions, eBay, or art auctions. Identify the format, discuss whether the assumptions of auction theory hold, and evaluate whether the design achieves its goals. Propose one improvement.
tasks.output: ~500 word analysis of a real-world auction with proposed improvement.
checklist: The auction format is correctly identified.
Theory assumptions are checked against reality.
The proposed improvement is specific and justified.

weeklySchedule.topic: Signaling Games

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 16: Signaling Games
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapter 16 on signaling and perfect Bayesian equilibrium. Focus on: the Spence education signaling model, pooling vs separating equilibria, the intuitive criterion, and cheap talk. Work through the labor market signaling model in detail.
tasks.output: Notes on signaling games, PBE, pooling/separating equilibria, and the Spence model.
checklist: Define perfect Bayesian equilibrium.
Distinguish pooling from separating equilibria.
Explain the Spence education model and its equilibria.

tasks.title: Polak Lectures 15-16: Signaling
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lectures 15 and 16 on signaling. Lecture 15 covers signaling in the labor market and strategic information transmission. Lecture 16 continues with signaling applications and the limits of signaling. Note how beliefs are updated using Bayes' rule on the equilibrium path.
tasks.output: Notes on signaling models, belief updating, and applications.
checklist: Show belief updating using Bayes' rule.
Identify pooling and separating equilibria in the labor market model.
Note when signaling is wasteful vs informative.

tasks.title: Practice: Signaling game analysis
tasks.prompt: Solve 4 signaling games: (1) Spence education model with 2 types, find all PBE. (2) A product quality signaling game (warranty as signal). (3) A political signaling game (campaign spending as signal). (4) A cheap talk game. For each, specify the game tree, find pooling and separating equilibria, and check the intuitive criterion.
tasks.output: 4 solved signaling games with PBE identified and refined.
checklist: Game trees are drawn for each signaling game.
Both pooling and separating equilibria are found where they exist.
The intuitive criterion is applied to eliminate unreasonable equilibria.

tasks.title: Response: Education as signaling vs human capital
tasks.prompt: In ~500 words, discuss the debate between education as signaling (Spence) vs education as human capital formation. What are the empirical implications of each? How would you design a study to distinguish them? Discuss policy implications of each view.
tasks.output: ~500 word analysis of the signaling vs human capital debate.
checklist: Both theories are stated clearly.
Empirical implications are contrasted.
Policy implications differ between the two views.

weeklySchedule.topic: Mechanism Design

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 17: Mechanism Design
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapter 17 on mechanism design. Focus on: the revelation principle, incentive compatibility, individual rationality, the VCG mechanism, and Myerson's optimal auction. Understand how mechanism design inverts the game theory question.
tasks.output: Notes on mechanism design, revelation principle, VCG, and optimal auctions.
checklist: Explain the reversal: designing games vs analyzing them.
State the revelation principle.
Describe the VCG mechanism and its properties.

tasks.title: Polak Lecture 17: Mechanism Design
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lecture 17 on mechanism design. Focus on how to design rules that elicit truthful information. Note the connection to auction theory and the VCG mechanism.
tasks.output: Notes on mechanism design principles and VCG.
checklist: The revelation principle is explained.
VCG is described with an example.
The connection to auction theory is noted.

tasks.title: Practice: Mechanism design problems
tasks.prompt: Solve 4 mechanism design problems: (1) Design a direct revelation mechanism for a bilateral trade problem (Myerson-Satterthwaite). (2) Implement a VCG mechanism for a public goods problem. (3) Find Myerson's optimal auction for 2 bidders with uniform valuations. (4) Design a mechanism for a kidney exchange problem. For each, check incentive compatibility and individual rationality.
tasks.output: 4 designed mechanisms with IC and IR verified.
checklist: Each mechanism is specified as a game with rules.
Incentive compatibility is verified.
Individual rationality is checked.

tasks.title: Response: Mechanism design and society
tasks.prompt: In ~500 words, discuss mechanism design as a tool for social engineering. Consider applications: voting systems, market design (kidney exchange, school choice), spectrum allocation. What are the limits of mechanism design? When does it fail? Consider computational complexity and strategic manipulation.
tasks.output: ~500 word essay on mechanism design applications and limitations.
checklist: At least two real applications are discussed.
Limitations of mechanism design are identified.
Computational or strategic challenges are addressed.

weeklySchedule.topic: Cooperative Games and the Shapley Value

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 18: Cooperative Games
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis Chapter 18 on cooperative game theory. Focus on: characteristic function form, the core, the Shapley value, and the Nash bargaining solution. Understand the difference between cooperative and non-cooperative approaches and when each is appropriate.
tasks.output: Notes on cooperative games, the core, and the Shapley value with examples.
checklist: Define characteristic function form.
Explain the core and when it is non-empty.
Compute the Shapley value for a 3-player example.

tasks.title: Polak Lecture 18: Cooperative Games
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lecture 18 on cooperative games. Note the shift from strategic to coalitional thinking. Focus on the Shapley value and its axiomatic derivation. Consider the application to voting power indices.
tasks.output: Notes on cooperative games, Shapley value axioms, and voting power.
checklist: The Shapley value axioms are listed.
A voting power example is computed.
The contrast with non-cooperative theory is noted.

tasks.title: Practice: Cooperative game solutions
tasks.prompt: Solve 5 cooperative game problems: (1) Compute the Shapley value for a 3-player game with a specific characteristic function. (2) Find the core of a 3-player cooperative game. (3) Compute the Banzhaf power index for a weighted voting game. (4) Analyze a cost-sharing problem using the Shapley value. (5) Check whether the core of a glove game is non-empty.
tasks.output: 5 solved cooperative game problems with Shapley values and core analysis.
checklist: Shapley values are computed using all permutations.
The core is found and checked for non-emptiness.
Power indices are computed correctly.

tasks.title: Response: Final project proposal
tasks.prompt: Write a ~500 word proposal for your final project. Choose ONE: (A) Model a real-world strategic situation as a game and solve it. (B) Survey a game theory topic beyond the syllabus (e.g., evolutionary game theory, algorithmic game theory, political game theory). (C) Replicate and critique an experimental game theory paper. Specify your topic, the game/model you will analyze, and the key questions you will address.
tasks.output: ~500 word final project proposal with topic, model, and key questions.
checklist: The topic is specific and scoped appropriately.
The model or approach is identified.
Key questions are clear and answerable.

weeklySchedule.topic: Evolutionary Game Theory

tasks.title: SEP: Evolutionary Game Theory + Tadelis review
tasks.prompt: Read the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on evolutionary game theory (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/game-evolutionary/). Focus on: the replicator dynamic, evolutionary stable strategies (ESS), and the relationship between evolutionary and rationalistic game theory. Also review Tadelis sections on evolutionary stability.
tasks.output: Notes on ESS, replicator dynamics, and the connection to Nash equilibrium.
checklist: Define ESS and relate it to Nash equilibrium.
Explain the replicator dynamic.
Note one application to biology and one to social science.

tasks.title: Polak Lectures 19-20: Evolutionary Stability
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lectures 19 and 20 on evolutionary stability. Focus on how strategies fare against mutations, the hawk-dove game, and the evolutionary interpretation of mixed strategies. Note how ESS refines Nash equilibrium.
tasks.output: Notes on ESS, hawk-dove game, and evolutionary refinement of Nash equilibrium.
checklist: The hawk-dove game is analyzed and solved.
ESS is shown to be a refinement of Nash equilibrium.
The biological interpretation of mixed strategies is explained.

tasks.title: Practice: Evolutionary stability
tasks.prompt: Solve 4 evolutionary game theory problems: (1) Find all ESS in the hawk-dove game. (2) Check whether the Nash equilibria of the Stag Hunt are ESS. (3) Analyze the replicator dynamic for the coordination game and identify stable fixed points. (4) Consider a 3-strategy game (Rock-Paper-Scissors) and analyze its evolutionary dynamics.
tasks.output: 4 solved evolutionary game problems with ESS and stability analysis.
checklist: ESS conditions are checked for each candidate strategy.
Replicator dynamics are set up and fixed points found.
Stability of fixed points is analyzed.

tasks.title: Response: Final project working draft
tasks.prompt: Submit a working draft of your final project. If modeling a game: present the model, solve for equilibrium, and discuss results. If a survey: outline all sections with key arguments. If a replication: present the experimental design and your preliminary findings. This should be at least 1000 words or equivalent.
tasks.output: Working draft of final project (1000+ words or equivalent).
checklist: The model or analysis is clearly presented.
Equilibrium/results are derived or preliminary findings are stated.
The draft is structured with clear sections.

weeklySchedule.topic: Applications and Final Project

tasks.title: Tadelis Ch. 19-20: Applications and Frontiers
tasks.prompt: Read Tadelis remaining chapters on applications. Focus on: political economy applications (voting, lobbying), industrial organization (entry, R&D races), and network effects. Also review the SEP game theory entry sections you have not yet read for philosophical perspectives.
tasks.output: Notes on applications across economics, political science, and philosophy.
checklist: At least 3 application areas are summarized.
The philosophical perspective on game theory is noted.
Connections between topics in the course are identified.

tasks.title: Polak Lectures 21-23: Applications and Wrap-up
tasks.prompt: Watch Yale ECON 159 Lectures 21-23 covering asymmetric information, signaling and suffering education, and course wrap-up. These lectures integrate multiple concepts. Note how signaling, moral hazard, and mechanism design connect.
tasks.output: Notes on asymmetric information applications and course integration.
checklist: The integration of signaling and mechanism design is explained.
At least one new application is noted.
Key takeaways from the full course are listed.

tasks.title: Practice: Comprehensive review problems
tasks.prompt: Complete a comprehensive final problem set covering all course topics. Solve: (1) A static game requiring Nash and mixed equilibrium. (2) A dynamic game requiring SPE. (3) A Bayesian game requiring BNE. (4) A signaling game requiring PBE. (5) A cooperative game requiring the Shapley value. These are your final exam preparation problems.
tasks.output: 5 comprehensive solved problems covering all major solution concepts.
checklist: Each problem uses a different solution concept.
All calculations are shown step by step.
Solutions are verified by checking for profitable deviations.

tasks.title: Final project submission and course reflection
tasks.prompt: Submit your final project (2000+ words or equivalent). Include: model/analysis, results, discussion of limitations, and connections to course material. Then write a ~400 word course reflection: What did you learn? How has game theory changed your thinking? What would you study next?
tasks.output: Final project (2000+ words) plus ~400 word course reflection.
checklist: The final project is complete with all required sections.
Limitations are honestly discussed.
The reflection connects to future learning goals.

title: CRWR 201: Worldbuilding
subject: Creative Writing
description: A mixed theory and practice course on constructing imaginary worlds for fiction, games, and transmedia. Study the history and theory of subcreation from Tolkien to modern franchise worldbuilding, then build your own world through a semester-long portfolio project. Read foundational texts, watch craft lectures, and produce worldbuilding documents weekly.
objectives: Define worldbuilding as a creative practice and distinguish it from setting, plot, and character.
Analyze existing imaginary worlds across literature, film, games, and other media using critical frameworks.
Construct a coherent fictional world with internal consistency across geography, history, culture, politics, and belief systems.
Design magic systems or technological frameworks that serve narrative rather than undermine it.
Apply techniques for revealing world information through scene and action rather than exposition dumps.
Evaluate the ethical and cultural implications of worldbuilding choices, including representation and appropriation.
Produce a comprehensive worldbuilding portfolio ready for use in a novel, game, or other creative project.

resources.label: Wonderbook (Revised and Expanded) by Jeff VanderMeer
resources.note: Primary textbook. Illustrated guide to creating imaginative fiction. Use the revised expanded edition (2018).

resources.label: Building Imaginary Worlds: The Theory and History of Subcreation by Mark J.P. Wolf
resources.note: Academic study of worldbuilding across media. Published by Routledge, 2012.

resources.label: How to Write Science Fiction and Fantasy by Orson Scott Card
resources.note: Full text available on Internet Archive. Chapter 2 (World Creation) is the core reading.

resources.label: Tolkien: On Fairy-Stories
resources.note: Tolkien's seminal 1947 essay on subcreation and secondary worlds. Free PDF from Internet Archive.

resources.label: 30 Days of Worldbuilding by A. Trevena
resources.note: Practical step-by-step workbook. Use as a companion for the portfolio project.

resources.label: Brandon Sanderson BYU Creative Writing Lectures (2020)
resources.note: Full university course on writing SF and fantasy. Lectures 5-8 focus on worldbuilding and magic systems.

resources.label: Hello Future Me (YouTube channel)
resources.note: Video essays on worldbuilding, including the 'Worldbuilding 101 and Beyond' playlist.

resources.label: Hello Future Me: Hard Worldbuilding vs. Soft Worldbuilding
resources.note: Key video essay contrasting hard and soft worldbuilding approaches, using Studio Ghibli as case study.

resources.label: Sanderson Lecture #5: Worldbuilding Part One
resources.note: First half of Sanderson's worldbuilding lectures from his BYU course.

resources.label: Sanderson Lecture #6: Worldbuilding Part Two
resources.note: Second half of Sanderson's worldbuilding lectures.

resources.label: Sanderson Lecture #7: Sanderson's Laws of Magic (2025)
resources.note: Lecture on magic system design and Sanderson's three laws.

resources.label: Sanderson Lecture #8: The Tools to Make Your Worlds Better (2025)
resources.note: Practical worldbuilding tools and revision techniques.

resources.label: Hello Future Me: Magic Systems and Handling Power Escalation
resources.note: Video essay on magic system design using Mistborn, Last Airbender, and Naruto as case studies.

resources.label: RIT Center for Worldbuilding and Storytelling: Course Catalog
resources.note: Reference: university worldbuilding course descriptions for comparison.

weeklySchedule.topic: What is worldbuilding? Subcreation and secondary worlds

tasks.title: Tolkien: On Fairy-Stories
tasks.prompt: Read Tolkien's essay. Focus on his definitions of Fantasy, Sub-creation, and the Secondary World. Identify the four functions he describes: Fantasy, Recovery, Escape, and Consolation. Write down one passage that defines subcreation and paraphrase it in your own words.
tasks.output: Notes with at least 3 key terms defined, one quoted passage, and one question.
checklist: Quote and page-reference one passage on sub-creation.
Define Fantasy, Recovery, Escape, and Consolation in your own words.
Note one question or objection about Tolkien's framework.

tasks.title: Wolf: Building Imaginary Worlds, Introduction and Chapter 1
tasks.prompt: Read the introduction and Chapter 1. Identify Wolf's definition of an imaginary world and how it differs from a setting. List the three qualities Wolf says make a world immersive and consistent.
tasks.output: Notes distinguishing world from setting, listing Wolf's key qualities, and one discussion question.
checklist: State Wolf's definition of an imaginary world.
List at least 3 qualities of immersive worlds from the text.
Note one point of agreement or disagreement with Tolkien's framework.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture #1: Introduction to Writing SF and Fantasy
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's introductory lecture. Note his framing of worldbuilding as one of five pillars of storytelling. Record his chef vs. cook analogy and what it means for worldbuilders.
tasks.output: One paragraph on Sanderson's framework and one question it raises for you.
checklist: Identify Sanderson's five pillars.
State the chef vs. cook analogy in your own words.
Note one practical takeaway for your own worldbuilding.

tasks.title: Reading response 1: What is a world?
tasks.prompt: In 300-400 words, define worldbuilding in your own terms using insights from Tolkien, Wolf, and Sanderson. Distinguish worldbuilding from setting, plot, and character. Give one example of a fictional world you know well and explain what makes it a world rather than just a backdrop.
tasks.output: ~350 words in your external workspace.
tasks.documentName: W01 - Response 01: What is a world?
checklist: Definition draws on at least two of the three readings.
Distinction between world and setting is explicit.
Example is specific and analytical, not just summary.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Concept seed
tasks.prompt: Write a 200-300 word concept document for the world you want to build this semester. What genre? What is the core premise or conflict? What makes this world different from ours? This is your starting point, not your final vision.
tasks.output: 200-300 word concept document.
checklist: Core premise is stated in one sentence.
Genre or tone is identified.
At least one element that distinguishes this world from ours.

weeklySchedule.topic: Hard vs. soft worldbuilding: the spectrum of specificity

tasks.title: Card: How to Write SF and Fantasy, Chapter 2 (World Creation)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 2. Focus on Card's 'idea net' method, his approach to rules of time, space, and magic, and his advice on history, language, geography, and customs. Note one technique you want to try in your own worldbuilding.
tasks.output: Notes on Card's idea net, rules framework, and one technique to apply.
checklist: Describe the 'idea net' in your own words.
List Card's categories of worldbuilding (history, language, geography, customs).
Note one technique you plan to apply to your portfolio.

tasks.title: Hello Future Me: Hard vs. Soft Worldbuilding
tasks.prompt: Watch the video essay. Define hard and soft worldbuilding in your own words. Identify one example of each from media you know. Which approach fits your concept seed from Week 1?
tasks.output: Notes with definitions, two examples, and a statement on your preferred approach.
checklist: Hard and soft worldbuilding are each defined.
One example of each approach from existing media.
A statement on which approach fits your portfolio world.

tasks.title: Wonderbook: Chapter 6 (Worldbuilding)
tasks.prompt: Read the worldbuilding chapter of Wonderbook. Note VanderMeer's distinction between worldbuilding as scaffolding vs. worldbuilding as ecosystem. Pick one exercise from the chapter and try it on your concept seed.
tasks.output: Notes on scaffolding vs. ecosystem, plus one exercise attempt.
checklist: Scaffolding vs. ecosystem distinction is clear.
At least one exercise from the chapter is attempted.
Note one way VanderMeer's approach differs from Card's.

tasks.title: Reading response 2: Where does your world sit?
tasks.prompt: In 300-400 words, analyze where your planned world falls on the hard-to-soft spectrum. What details need to be hard (specific, rule-bound) and what can be soft (atmospheric, impressionistic)? Justify your choices using insights from Card, VanderMeer, and the Hello Future Me video.
tasks.output: ~350 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Position on the spectrum is stated and justified.
At least two sources are referenced.
Specific elements of your world are assigned to hard or soft treatment.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Core rules and axioms
tasks.prompt: Write 5-10 core rules or axioms for your world. These are the foundational principles that everything else hangs on: physical laws, magical laws, social laws, or cosmological laws. Each rule should be one sentence. Beneath each, write one sentence on why it matters.
tasks.output: 5-10 rules with justifications.
checklist: At least 5 rules are stated.
Each rule has a one-sentence justification.
Rules are consistent with your Week 1 concept seed.

weeklySchedule.topic: Worldbuilding as narrative tool: setting as character

tasks.title: Wolf: Building Imaginary Worlds, Chapter 2 (History of Imaginary Worlds)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 2 on the history of imaginary worlds from Homer to modern franchises. Identify three turning points in how humans have built imaginary worlds. Note how media changes affected worldbuilding practice.
tasks.output: Notes with three historical turning points and one observation on media influence.
tasks.documentName: W03 - Wolf: History of imaginary worlds
checklist: Three turning points are identified with approximate dates.
At least one observation on how media changes worldbuilding.
One question about historical patterns in worldbuilding.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture #5: Worldbuilding Part One
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's first worldbuilding lecture. Note his framework for how worldbuilding interacts with plot and character. Record his advice on what to build vs. what to imply.
tasks.output: Notes on Sanderson's worldbuilding framework and one technique to apply.
checklist: Sanderson's framework for worldbuilding is summarized.
Advice on building vs. implying is noted.
One technique is identified for your portfolio.

tasks.title: Reading response 3: The world serves the story
tasks.prompt: In 300-400 words, argue for or against the claim that worldbuilding should always serve narrative. Use examples from at least two worlds you know (books, films, games, or TTRPGs). Consider cases where worldbuilding overshadows story versus cases where it elevates it.
tasks.output: ~350 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Position is stated clearly.
At least two example worlds are analyzed.
Counter-argument is addressed.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Core locations
tasks.prompt: Write 1-2 paragraphs each for three core locations in your world. For each location, describe: its physical appearance, its emotional tone, one sensory detail, and one narrative hook (something that could generate a story). Draw a rough sketch map if helpful.
tasks.output: Three location descriptions with sensory details and narrative hooks.
checklist: Three locations are described with physical and emotional detail.
Each has at least one sensory detail.
Each has a narrative hook that could drive a story.

weeklySchedule.topic: Geography, maps, and environments

tasks.title: Wonderbook: Environment and ecology sections
tasks.prompt: Read the sections of Wonderbook covering environment, ecology, and natural worldbuilding. Note VanderMeer's advice on how geography shapes culture and how ecosystems create narrative constraints.
tasks.output: Notes on environment-creating-culture principles and one ecosystem idea for your world.
checklist: At least one principle about geography shaping culture is noted.
One ecosystem idea is generated for your portfolio.
A question or area to explore further is recorded.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture #6: Worldbuilding Part Two
