tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's second worldbuilding lecture. Focus on his advice about physical worldbuilding, resources, and how geography creates conflict. Note one resource or geographic feature that could drive conflict in your world.
tasks.output: Notes on geographic conflict drivers and one idea for your world.
checklist: Sanderson's advice on geography-as-conflict is summarized.
One geographic conflict driver is identified for your world.
A practical technique from the lecture is noted.

tasks.title: 30 Days of Worldbuilding: Days 1-5 (geography prompts)
tasks.prompt: Work through days 1-5 of the 30 Days of Worldbuilding workbook. These cover basic geography, climate, and natural features. Complete the prompts for your world.
tasks.output: Completed workbook prompts for days 1-5.
checklist: All five daily prompts are completed.
Climate and terrain are consistent with your core rules.
At least one geographic feature could serve as a narrative setting.

tasks.title: Portfolio: World map sketch
tasks.prompt: Create a sketch map of your world or your core region. Include major landmasses, water bodies, mountain ranges, and at least three settlements. Label geographic features with provisional names. The map can be hand-drawn and scanned, or created digitally. Write a 200-word caption explaining your design choices.
tasks.output: A sketch map (image file) and a 200-word design rationale.
checklist: Map includes landmasses, water, and mountains.
At least three settlements are marked.
Design rationale explains at least two geographic choices.

tasks.title: Reading response 4: How geography shapes story
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, analyze how geography shapes story in one fictional world you know well. Identify one geographic feature that creates narrative conflict or opportunity. Then describe one geographic feature in your own world and the story it could generate.
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: One existing world is analyzed for geographic storytelling.
One geographic feature in your own world is described.
The narrative potential of that feature is explained.

weeklySchedule.topic: History, timelines, and deep time

tasks.title: Wolf: Building Imaginary Worlds, Chapter 3 (Narrative and Internarrative Theory)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 3 on how narratives structure worlds and how multiple narratives interact within a single world. Note Wolf's concepts of retroactive continuity, multiverses, and how history functions differently in worlds vs. stories.
tasks.output: Notes on internarrative theory, retcon, and how history works in worlds.
checklist: Internarrative theory is summarized.
At least one concept (retcon, multiverse) is defined.
A question about history in your own world is recorded.

tasks.title: Card: How to Write SF and Fantasy, history and customs sections
tasks.prompt: Re-read Card's sections on working out the history of your world. Note his advice on what to develop vs. what to sketch. Identify one historical event that will shape your world's present.
tasks.output: Notes on Card's approach to history and one key historical event for your world.
checklist: Card's approach to history is summarized.
One key historical event for your world is identified.
The event's impact on the present is noted.

tasks.title: 30 Days of Worldbuilding: Days 6-10 (history and culture prompts)
tasks.prompt: Work through days 6-10 of the workbook, covering history, broad cultural strokes, and societal foundations. Complete the prompts for your world.
tasks.output: Completed workbook prompts for days 6-10.
checklist: All five daily prompts are completed.
At least one major historical event is established.
History is consistent with your geography from Week 4.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Historical timeline
tasks.prompt: Create a timeline of at least 10 major events in your world's history. Include founding events, conflicts, technological or magical developments, and cultural shifts. For each event, write one sentence on its ongoing impact on the present day of your world.
tasks.output: A timeline with 10+ events and impact notes.
checklist: At least 10 events are listed in chronological order.
Each event has a one-sentence present-day impact.
Timeline is consistent with geography and core rules.

tasks.title: Reading response 5: The iceberg principle
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, describe how much of your world's history a reader or player needs to know versus how much you need to build. Use the metaphor of the iceberg (visible tip vs. hidden mass). Give one example from a world you admire where deep history enhances the surface story.
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Visible vs. hidden history is distinguished.
One admired world is cited as example.
Your own world's iceberg ratio is stated.

weeklySchedule.topic: Languages, naming, and constructed languages

tasks.title: Wonderbook: Language and voice sections
tasks.prompt: Read the sections of Wonderbook on language, voice, and naming. Note VanderMeer's advice on how naming conventions reveal culture and how invented language fragments create texture without requiring full conlangs.
tasks.output: Notes on naming conventions and language-as-texture.
checklist: Naming convention principles are noted.
At least one naming idea for your world is recorded.
A question about language in your world is noted.

tasks.title: Card: How to Write SF and Fantasy, language section
tasks.prompt: Re-read Card's section on language in worldbuilding. Note his caution about invented jargon and his advice on using language sparingly but effectively. Identify one principle you will follow in naming your world's places and people.
tasks.output: Notes on Card's language principles and one naming rule for your world.
checklist: Card's caution on jargon is noted.
One naming principle for your world is stated.
A potential pitfall in your naming scheme is identified.

tasks.title: Hello Future Me: Worldbuilding playlist, naming and culture videos
tasks.prompt: Watch one or two videos from Hello Future Me's Worldbuilding 101 playlist on naming or culture. Note how naming systems reflect cultural values and power structures.
tasks.output: Notes on naming-as-cultural-signifier and one technique for your world.
checklist: At least one naming technique is noted.
Connection between naming and culture is stated.
One application to your own world is recorded.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Naming guide and language fragments
tasks.prompt: Create a naming guide for your world. Include: naming conventions for at least two cultures (how personal names, place names, and institutional names are formed), 5-10 place names using your conventions, and 10-20 vocabulary words from one constructed language or dialect. Write a 200-word note on how naming reflects culture.
tasks.output: Naming guide with conventions, examples, and language fragments.
tasks.documentName: W06 - Naming guide and language fragments
checklist: Naming conventions for at least two cultures are documented.
10+ place names follow the conventions.
10+ vocabulary words are provided with meanings.

tasks.title: Reading response 6: What's in a name?
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, analyze the naming system of one fictional world you know. How do names reflect culture, history, or power? Then critique your own naming guide: what does it reveal about your world's cultures, and what might it unintentionally signal?
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
tasks.documentName: W06 - Response 06: What's in a name?
checklist: One existing world's naming system is analyzed.
Your own naming guide is self-critiqued.
At least one unintended signal in your naming is identified.

weeklySchedule.topic: Cultures, customs, and daily life

tasks.title: Wonderbook: Culture and society sections
tasks.prompt: Read the sections of Wonderbook covering culture, society, and character-as-product-of-culture. Note how VanderMeer connects daily life to worldbuilding and how small details (food, clothing, ritual) build immersion.
tasks.output: Notes on daily-life-as-worldbuilding and three cultural details to develop.
checklist: Daily-life worldbuilding principles are noted.
Three cultural details to develop are listed.
A connection between culture and your core rules is noted.

tasks.title: 30 Days of Worldbuilding: Days 11-15 (culture and society prompts)
tasks.prompt: Work through days 11-15 of the workbook, covering cultural details, daily life, and social structures. Complete the prompts for your world.
tasks.output: Completed workbook prompts for days 11-15.
checklist: All five daily prompts are completed.
Daily life details are consistent with geography and history.
At least one custom or ritual is fully described.

tasks.title: Hello Future Me: Cultural worldbuilding videos
tasks.prompt: Watch one video from Hello Future Me on cultural worldbuilding (e.g., analysis of Avatar: The Last Airbender's cultures or similar). Note how cultures are built from environment plus history plus values.
tasks.output: Notes on the environment-history-values framework and one application.
checklist: The environment-history-values framework is summarized.
One application to your world is described.
A question about your world's cultures is noted.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Culture document
tasks.prompt: Write a 500-700 word culture document for one major culture in your world. Cover: daily life (food, work, family structure), one major custom or ritual, clothing and material culture, values and taboos, and how the culture's environment shaped these traits.
tasks.output: 500-700 word culture document.
checklist: Daily life is described with specific details.
At least one custom or ritual is fully described.
Environment-culture connection is explicit.

tasks.title: Reading response 7: Culture is not costume
tasks.prompt: In 300-400 words, discuss the ethical responsibility of worldbuilders when creating fictional cultures. What is the difference between inspiration and appropriation? Identify one risk in your own culture document and how you plan to address it.
tasks.output: ~350 words in your external workspace.
tasks.documentName: W07 - Response 07: Culture is not costume
checklist: Inspiration vs. appropriation is distinguished.
One risk in your own work is identified.
A concrete plan to address the risk is stated.

weeklySchedule.topic: Politics, power structures, and economics

tasks.title: Card: How to Write SF and Fantasy, customs and social structures
tasks.prompt: Re-read Card's sections on customs and social structures. Note his advice on how power structures create story potential and how economic systems shape daily life. Identify one power structure for your world.
tasks.output: Notes on power-as-story-generator and one power structure for your world.
checklist: Card's approach to social structures is summarized.
One power structure for your world is identified.
The narrative potential of that structure is noted.

tasks.title: 30 Days of Worldbuilding: Days 16-20 (politics and economics prompts)
tasks.prompt: Work through days 16-20 of the workbook, covering political structures, economic systems, and power dynamics. Complete the prompts for your world.
tasks.output: Completed workbook prompts for days 16-20.
checklist: All five daily prompts are completed.
Political structure is consistent with culture and history.
At least one source of political conflict is identified.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture #8: Tools to Make Your Worlds Better
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's tools lecture. Note his practical techniques for building political and social systems that generate conflict. Record one tool you will apply to your political structure.
tasks.output: Notes on Sanderson's worldbuilding tools and one application.
checklist: At least one practical tool from the lecture is noted.
One application to your world's politics is described.
A conflict generator is identified.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Political and economic document
tasks.prompt: Write a 500-700 word document covering: the political system of one region in your world, who holds power and why, one economic system (trade, currency, production), and at least two factions or interest groups in tension. Identify one conflict that could drive a story.
tasks.output: 500-700 word political and economic document.
checklist: Political system is described with power holders identified.
Economic system is described.
At least two factions in tension are named.
One story-driving conflict is identified.

tasks.title: Reading response 8: Power creates plot
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, analyze how a political system in one fictional world you know generates narrative conflict. Then identify one conflict in your own political document and describe the story it could drive.
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: One existing world's politics-as-plot is analyzed.
One conflict in your own world is identified.
The story potential of that conflict is described.

weeklySchedule.topic: Religion, mythology, and belief systems

tasks.title: Wonderbook: Myth and belief sections
tasks.prompt: Read the sections of Wonderbook on myth, belief, and the numinous in worldbuilding. Note how VanderMeer treats religion as worldbuilding infrastructure rather than decoration.
tasks.output: Notes on religion-as-infrastructure and one belief system idea.
checklist: Religion-as-infrastructure concept is noted.
One belief system idea for your world is recorded.
A question about belief in your world is noted.

tasks.title: 30 Days of Worldbuilding: Days 21-25 (religion and belief prompts)
tasks.prompt: Work through days 21-25 of the workbook, covering religion, mythology, and belief systems. Complete the prompts for your world.
tasks.output: Completed workbook prompts for days 21-25.
checklist: All five daily prompts are completed.
Belief system is consistent with culture and history.
At least one myth or origin story is written.

tasks.title: Revisit Tolkien: On Fairy-Stories (Consolation and Eucatastrophe sections)
tasks.prompt: Re-read Tolkien's sections on Consolation and the Eucatastrophe. Consider how belief systems in your world could provide narrative consolation or catastrophic turns. Write one paragraph on how your world's mythology serves its story.
tasks.output: One paragraph on mythology-as-narrative-tool in your world.
checklist: Eucatastrophe is defined in your own words.
Mythology's narrative function in your world is described.
Connection to Tolkien's Consolation is made.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Religion and mythology document
tasks.prompt: Write a 500-700 word document covering: one major belief system in your world (deities or cosmic principles, if any), one origin myth or creation story (200+ words), one major ritual or holy day, and how the belief system shapes daily life and politics. Write the creation myth in an in-world voice.
tasks.output: 500-700 word religion and mythology document with an in-world creation myth.
checklist: Belief system is described with cosmology.
Creation myth is 200+ words in an in-world voice.
At least one ritual or holy day is described.
Belief-politics connection is noted.

tasks.title: Reading response 9: Belief as worldbuilding engine
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, analyze how one fictional world's belief system drives plot or character. Consider how belief creates conflict, motivates characters, or shapes world events. Then identify one way your own belief system could generate a story.
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: One existing world's belief system is analyzed.
Your own belief system's story potential is identified.
The analysis connects belief to plot or character.

weeklySchedule.topic: Magic systems and Sanderson's Laws

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture #7: Sanderson's Laws of Magic
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's lecture on magic systems. Record all three laws verbatim and then paraphrase each. Note the distinction between hard and soft magic systems and when each is appropriate.
tasks.output: Notes with all three laws, paraphrases, and hard/soft magic distinction.
checklist: All three laws are quoted and paraphrased.
Hard vs. soft magic distinction is clear.
One law is identified as most relevant to your world.

tasks.title: Hello Future Me: Magic Systems and Power Escalation
tasks.prompt: Watch the video essay on magic systems. Note how power escalation is managed (or mismanaged) in the case studies. Identify one principle for keeping magic systems balanced over a long narrative.
tasks.output: Notes on power escalation management and one balancing principle.
tasks.documentName: W10 - HFM: Magic and power escalation
checklist: At least one power escalation principle is noted.
One case study from the video is summarized.
A balancing principle for your world is identified.

tasks.title: Card: How to Write SF and Fantasy, rules of magic section
tasks.prompt: Re-read Card's section on the rules of magic. Note his advice on consistency, cost, and limitation. Identify one cost or limitation for your magic system.
tasks.output: Notes on Card's magic rules and one cost/limitation for your system.
checklist: Card's approach to magic rules is summarized.
One cost or limitation for your system is stated.
Consistency with your core rules is checked.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Magic system document
tasks.prompt: Write a 500-700 word magic system document covering: the source of magic in your world, what magic can do (3-5 specific abilities), what it cannot do (hard limits), the cost of using magic (physical, social, or spiritual), and how magic affects politics and daily life. Apply Sanderson's First Law explicitly.
tasks.output: 500-700 word magic system document.
checklist: Source of magic is defined.
3-5 abilities and hard limits are listed.
Cost of magic is specified.
Sanderson's First Law is explicitly applied.
Political/social impact is noted.

tasks.title: Reading response 10: The cost of magic
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, analyze the cost structure of one magic system you know well. How do costs create narrative tension? Then evaluate your own magic system: is the cost meaningful enough to drive stories? If not, propose one revision.
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: One existing magic system's costs are analyzed.
Your own system's costs are evaluated.
At least one revision is proposed if needed.

weeklySchedule.topic: Technology, science, and speculative systems

tasks.title: Wonderbook: Technology and extrapolation sections
tasks.prompt: Read the sections of Wonderbook on technology, extrapolation, and speculative science. Note how VanderMeer distinguishes hard SF extrapolation from softer approaches. Identify one technology or scientific principle for your world.
tasks.output: Notes on extrapolation methods and one technology for your world.
checklist: Extrapolation vs. softer approaches are distinguished.
One technology or principle for your world is identified.
A question about tech's impact on your world is noted.

tasks.title: 30 Days of Worldbuilding: Days 26-30 (final integration prompts)
tasks.prompt: Work through the final days 26-30 of the workbook, covering technology, integration, and world assembly. Complete the prompts for your world.
tasks.output: Completed workbook prompts for days 26-30.
checklist: All five daily prompts are completed.
Technology is consistent with your world's rules.
Integration of all systems is attempted.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture #5 or #6 (revisit): systems integration
tasks.prompt: Re-watch a 30-minute segment of one Sanderson worldbuilding lecture, focusing on how systems interact. Note how magic, technology, politics, and geography form an ecosystem. Identify one interaction in your own world you have not yet explored.
tasks.output: Notes on systems-as-ecosystem and one unexplored interaction.
checklist: Systems-as-ecosystem concept is noted.
One unexplored interaction in your world is identified.
A plan to develop that interaction is sketched.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Technology or systems document
tasks.prompt: Write a 400-600 word document covering one major technology or scientific system in your world. Describe what it does, who has access to it, how it was developed, and how it interacts with at least two other systems (magic, politics, economics, religion, or geography). If your world is pre-technological, write about a craft, infrastructure, or knowledge system instead.
tasks.output: 400-600 word technology or systems document.
checklist: One system is described with function and access.
Development history is sketched.
At least two cross-system interactions are described.

tasks.title: Reading response 11: The ecology of systems
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, describe one way that two systems in your world interact that you had not initially planned. How did building one system (e.g., magic) force you to rethink another (e.g., politics or economics)? What does this reveal about the interconnected nature of worldbuilding?
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: One unplanned system interaction is described.
The chain of cause-and-effect is traced.
A reflection on worldbuilding as interconnected is included.

weeklySchedule.topic: Integration: the ecology of your world

tasks.title: Wolf: Building Imaginary Worlds, Chapter 4 (Audience and Participatory Dynamics)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 4 on how audiences experience and participate in imaginary worlds. Note how consistency, incompleteness, and the invitation to fill gaps all shape audience engagement. Consider how your world invites participation.
tasks.output: Notes on audience engagement, consistency vs. gaps, and participatory design.
checklist: Audience engagement principles are noted.
Consistency vs. incompleteness tension is described.
One way your world invites participation is identified.

tasks.title: Analytical essay: Compare two worlds
tasks.prompt: Write a 1000-1200 word analytical essay comparing the worldbuilding approaches of two imaginary worlds from different media (e.g., a novel and a game, or a film and a TTRPG setting). Use Wolf's framework (consistency, incompleteness, audience participation) and at least one other source from the course. Analyze how each world's design choices serve its medium.
tasks.output: 1000-1200 word analytical essay.
checklist: Two worlds from different media are compared.
Wolf's framework is applied.
At least one other course source is referenced.
Medium-specific design choices are analyzed.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Integration audit
tasks.prompt: Review all your portfolio documents from Weeks 1-11. Write a 400-600 word integration audit identifying: three strengths of your world so far, three inconsistencies or gaps, and three connections between systems you want to develop further. This is a working document for the final portfolio push.
tasks.output: 400-600 word integration audit.
checklist: Three strengths are identified.
Three inconsistencies or gaps are listed.
Three connections to develop are described.

tasks.title: Reading response 12: Consistency vs. mystery
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, reflect on the tension Wolf identifies between consistency and incompleteness. How much of your world should be defined versus left mysterious? Give one example from your own world where deliberate mystery serves the story better than full explanation.
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: The tension between consistency and mystery is articulated.
One area of your world is designated as deliberately mysterious.
The narrative benefit of that mystery is explained.

weeklySchedule.topic: Revealing the world: exposition, show vs. tell

tasks.title: Card: How to Write SF and Fantasy, Chapter 4 (Writing Well / Exposition)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 4 on keeping exposition in its place. Note Card's techniques for leading readers into strangeness step by step. Identify one exposition problem in your own world and a technique to solve it.
tasks.output: Notes on exposition techniques and one problem-solution for your world.
checklist: At least two exposition techniques are noted.
One exposition problem in your world is identified.
A technique to solve it is described.

tasks.title: Wonderbook: Revision and worldbuilding integration sections
tasks.prompt: Read the sections of Wonderbook on revision, particularly how to integrate worldbuilding into prose without info-dumping. Note one revision technique for worldbuilding-heavy prose.
tasks.output: Notes on revision techniques and one technique to apply.
checklist: At least one revision technique is noted.
One technique to apply to your portfolio is identified.
An info-dumping risk in your world is flagged.

tasks.title: Hello Future Me: How to Master Pacing
tasks.prompt: Watch the pacing video essay. Note how pacing and worldbuilding revelation intersect. Identify one pacing principle for revealing your world gradually.
tasks.output: Notes on pacing-as-revelation and one principle for your world.
checklist: Pacing-as-revelation concept is noted.
One pacing principle for your world is stated.
A plan for gradual world revelation is sketched.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Opening scene
tasks.prompt: Write a 1000-1500 word opening scene set in your world. The scene must reveal at least three worldbuilding elements (geography, culture, magic, politics, or belief) through action and dialogue, not exposition. Show a character interacting with the world's systems. This is the creative capstone of your portfolio.
tasks.output: 1000-1500 word opening scene.
checklist: At least three worldbuilding elements are revealed.
Worldbuilding is shown through action and dialogue, not exposition.
A character interacts with at least one world system.
The scene has narrative tension or a hook.

tasks.title: Reading response 13: Show, don't tell the world
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, analyze one passage from a published work that reveals worldbuilding through scene rather than exposition. Quote the passage. Then identify one moment in your own opening scene where you told rather than showed, and propose a revision.
tasks.output: ~300 words with a quoted passage in your external workspace.
checklist: One published passage is quoted and analyzed.
One tell-not-show moment in your scene is identified.
A concrete revision is proposed.

weeklySchedule.topic: Portfolio workshop and revision

tasks.title: Wonderbook: Workshop and feedback sections
tasks.prompt: Read the sections of Wonderbook on workshopping and giving/receiving feedback. Note VanderMeer's principles for constructive critique. Identify one principle you will use when self-reviewing your portfolio.
tasks.output: Notes on workshop principles and one self-review principle.
checklist: At least two workshop principles are noted.
One self-review principle is stated.
A plan for revising your portfolio is sketched.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture #8 (revisit): Revision tools
tasks.prompt: Re-watch a 30-minute segment of Sanderson's tools lecture, focusing on revision. Note one revision tool for worldbuilding specifically and plan to apply it.
tasks.output: Notes on revision tools and one tool to apply.
checklist: At least one revision tool is noted.
A plan to apply it to your portfolio is described.
One specific section of your portfolio is targeted for revision.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Comprehensive revision
tasks.prompt: Revise your entire portfolio based on your Week 12 integration audit and your Week 13 scene. Address the three inconsistencies you identified, develop the three connections you wanted to explore, and ensure your opening scene's worldbuilding is consistent with your system documents. Write a 300-word revision summary listing every change made.
tasks.output: Revised portfolio documents and a 300-word revision summary.
checklist: All three inconsistencies from the audit are addressed.
All three connections are developed.
Opening scene is consistent with system documents.
Revision summary lists all changes.

tasks.title: Reading response 14: Self-critique
tasks.prompt: In 300 words, write an honest self-critique of your world. What is its strongest system? What is its weakest? What would you build next if you had another semester? What did you learn about your own worldbuilding tendencies, both strengths and blind spots?
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Strongest and weakest systems are identified.
Next steps are described.
Personal worldbuilding tendencies are reflected on.

weeklySchedule.topic: Final portfolio assembly and reflection

tasks.title: Portfolio: Final assembly
tasks.prompt: Assemble your final worldbuilding portfolio into a single coherent document. Include: concept seed, core rules, map, timeline, naming guide, culture document, political document, religion and mythology document, magic system document, technology document, opening scene, and revision summary. Add a table of contents and a one-paragraph world summary at the top. Ensure all documents are internally consistent.
tasks.output: Complete worldbuilding portfolio with table of contents.
checklist: All portfolio documents are included.
Table of contents is present.
One-paragraph world summary leads the document.
Internal consistency is verified across all sections.

tasks.title: Final reflection: The world you built

title: PHIL 102: Introduction to Ethics
subject: Philosophy
description: A question-driven introduction to ethical theory. Explore how philosophers have answered the question 'How should we live?' from ancient Greece to the present. Read primary texts by Aristotle, Kant, Mill, and others, reconstruct their arguments, test objections, and develop your own moral reasoning. Covers virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism, social contract theory, care ethics, and applied ethics.
objectives: Distinguish metaethics, normative ethics, and applied ethics as levels of moral inquiry.
Reconstruct the central arguments of major ethical theories including virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism, and social contract theory.
Evaluate competing ethical theories using thought experiments, counterexamples, and real-world cases.
Apply ethical frameworks to contemporary moral problems such as animal rights, environmental ethics, and bioethics.
Articulate and defend your own position on a moral question in clear, structured prose with textual evidence.
Identify the strengths and weaknesses of relativism, objectivism, and the relationship between religion and morality.

resources.label: Introduction to Philosophy: Ethics (Rebus/Open Textbook)
resources.note: Free open-access textbook. Chapters on relativism, divine command, virtue ethics, egoism, utilitarianism, Kantian deontology, feminist ethics, and evolutionary ethics.

resources.label: Introduction to Ethics: Thinking Through a Moral Life (TRU Open Press)
resources.note: Free OER textbook with primary texts, summaries, case studies from Ethics Bowl Canada, and a practical guide to reading and writing philosophy.

resources.label: Jeffrey Kaplan - Introduction to Ethics (YouTube)
resources.note: Full introductory ethics course (28 lectures). Covers Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes, Hume, Bentham, Kant, Nietzsche, Singer, O'Neill and others.

resources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
resources.note: Reference library; optional exploration, not a specific assigned reading.

resources.label: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
resources.note: Reference library; optional exploration, not a specific assigned reading.

resources.label: Aristotle - Nicomachean Ethics
resources.note: Project Gutenberg free text. Read Books I-II for virtue ethics foundations.

resources.label: Kant - Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals (Groundwork)
resources.note: Thomas Kingsmill Abbott translation. Read Section I and Section II.

resources.label: Mill - Utilitarianism
resources.note: Read Chapters II and IV.

resources.label: Mill - On Liberty
resources.note: Read Chapter I (Introductory) and Chapter II (Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion).

resources.label: Hobbes - Leviathan
resources.note: Read Chapters XIII-XVII for social contract theory foundations.

weeklySchedule.topic: What is ethics? Metaethics, normative ethics, and applied ethics

tasks.title: Rebus textbook: Introduction and Chapter 1 (Moral Relativism and Subjectivism)
tasks.prompt: Read the Introduction and Chapter 1 ('Aren't Right and Wrong Just Matters of Opinion?'). Write down the distinction between metaethics, normative ethics, and applied ethics. Identify one objection to moral relativism that you find compelling and one that you find weak.

tasks.title: Kaplan: Introduction to Ethics - What is morality?

Your own position is stated with reasoning.
At least one example from the reading is cited.

weeklySchedule.topic: Religion and ethics: Divine command theory and natural law

tasks.output: Notes with the Euthyphro dilemma reconstructed, DCT vs natural law distinguished, and your evaluation.

Your evaluation of the reply's success is explicit.

weeklySchedule.topic: Virtue ethics: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics

tasks.output: Notes on eudaimonia, the doctrine of the mean, and the table of virtues and vices.

tasks.output: Notes on Kaplan's explanation and one open question.

weeklySchedule.topic: Virtue ethics: Applications and objections

tasks.title: TRU textbook: Virtue ethics case studies and discussion questions
tasks.prompt: Read the TRU Open Press chapter on virtue ethics, including any case studies. Choose one case study and analyze it using Aristotle's framework. What would a virtuous person do, and why? Identify the relevant virtues and vices.
tasks.output: A case analysis (~200 words) applying Aristotle's virtues to a concrete scenario.

Relevant virtues and vices are named.

tasks.prompt: Write a first draft (~500 words) comparing virtue ethics and utilitarianism. Focus on how each theory would approach a moral dilemma (e.g., whether to lie to a friend to spare their feelings). What does each theory focus on, and what does it overlook? You will revise this in Week 5.

weeklySchedule.topic: Utilitarianism: Bentham and Mill

tasks.title: Mill: Utilitarianism, Chapters II and IV
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter II ('What Utilitarianism Is') and Chapter IV ('Of what sort of proof the principle of utility is susceptible'). title: IDST 350: Tabletop RPG Design
subject: Interdisciplinary Studies
description: A mixed-theory-and-practice course in tabletop roleplaying game design. Study game design theory from Schell, Salen & Zimmerman, Koster, and Fullerton, apply it to the TTRPG medium through close play and deconstruction of existing games, and build a complete mini-RPG through iterative prototyping and playtesting. Covers resolution mechanics, character systems, conflict design, scenario structure, worldbuilding, narrative mechanics, and indie publishing.
objectives: Apply game design theory (Schell's lenses, Rules/Play/Culture schema, Koster's theory of fun) to the specific medium of tabletop RPGs.
Analyze and deconstruct existing TTRPG resolution systems, character mechanics, and conflict models.
Design and iterate a core resolution mechanic with documented probability distributions.
Build a character creation system with meaningful progression choices.
Design conflict resolution rules that create tension without halting narrative momentum.
Structure scenarios using node-based design and revelation lists.
Create setting documents and adventure modules that are immediately playable.
Produce a complete, playtested mini-RPG (4-8 pages) with a design diary.

resources.label: Schell, The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses (3rd ed.)
resources.note: Primary textbook. Over 100 design lenses applicable to TTRPGs. Platform-agnostic.

resources.label: Fullerton, Game Design Workshop (5th ed.)
resources.note: Primary textbook. Playcentric design process: prototyping, playtesting, iteration.

resources.label: Salen & Zimmerman, Rules of Play (MIT Press, 2003)
resources.note: Free on Internet Archive. Foundational theoretical framework: games as rules, play, and culture.

resources.label: Costikyan, 'I Have No Words and I Must Design' (2002 revision)
resources.note: Free PDF. Foundational essay on critical vocabulary for game design.

resources.label: Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design (10th anniversary ed.)
resources.note: Classic on why games are fun and what they teach. Widely used in university game design programs.

resources.label: The Forge: Provisional Glossary (Big Model, GNS, Creative Agenda)
resources.note: Free. Foundational RPG design theory: Social Contract, Exploration, Creative Agenda, Techniques, Ephemera.

resources.label: The Alexandrian (Justin Alexander) - RPG Design Essays
resources.note: Free. Node-based scenario design, revelation lists, the Three Clue Rule, pacing, advanced gamemastery.

resources.label: Lumpley Games (Vincent Baker) - Design Blog
resources.note: Free. Indie RPG design theory, PbtA design principles, GNS revisited, system and credibility.

resources.label: Matt Colville - Running the Game (YouTube)
resources.note: Free. Practical GM advice, campaign structure, worldbuilding, encounter design. Search 'Running the Game' on YouTube for full playlist.

resources.label: Sarah Lynne Bowman - Indie TTRPG Design (YouTube)
resources.note: Free. Two-part lecture: indie RPG design basics, Fiasco, Apocalypse World, crowdfunding, community.

resources.label: RPG PHD (YouTube) - TTRPG Design Analysis
resources.note: Free. Dieter Rams' Ten Principles applied to TTRPG mechanics. Design clarity, usability, cognitive load.

resources.label: Honey Heist by Grant Howitt (itch.io, PWYW)
resources.note: Pay-what-you-want. One-page RPG. Excellent example of minimal design with maximum flavor.

resources.label: Lasers & Feelings by Naomi Norris (one-sevendesign)
resources.note: Free. One-page RPG. Classic example of a simple resolution mechanic driving distinct play styles.

resources.label: Mork Borg Bare Bones Edition (itch.io, free)
resources.note: Free. Full rules text without art. Study how aesthetic and tone are embedded in the rules themselves.

resources.label: Zagal & Deterding, Role-Playing Game Studies: Transmedia Foundations (Routledge, 2018)
resources.note: Academic reference. 50+ scholars cover RPG history, theory, and design. Library resource for deep dives.

resources.label: Costikyan & Davidson, Tabletop: Analog Game Design (ETC Press, 2011)
resources.note: Free. Essays by professional tabletop game designers on analog design principles. Library resource.

weeklySchedule.topic: What Is a Game? What Is an RPG?

tasks.title: Schell: The Designer, the Experience, the Game
tasks.prompt: Read Schell Ch 1-5 (In the Beginning There Is the Designer, The Designer Creates an Experience, The Experience Rises Out of a Game, The Game Consists of Elements, The Elements Support a Theme). Note how Schell defines the designer's role and the relationship between experience, game, and elements. For each chapter, write down one lens that applies to TTRPGs specifically.
tasks.output: Notes with 5 key concepts and 5 TTRPG-specific lens applications.
checklist: Each chapter has at least one noted concept.
Each TTRPG lens application is specific, not generic.
You can explain Schell's definition of 'experience' in your own words.

tasks.title: Costikyan: I Have No Words and I Must Design
tasks.prompt: Read Costikyan's essay. List his key vocabulary terms (decision-making, opposition, resources, token placement, information, color, simulation, variety, roleplaying, socializing, narrative). For each term, write one sentence on how it applies (or fails to apply) to TTRPGs.
tasks.output: Glossary of Costikyan's terms with TTRPG-specific annotations.
checklist: All key terms are listed.
Each TTRPG annotation is concrete, referencing a specific game if possible.
You can articulate what Costikyan means by 'a game is interactive.'

tasks.title: Colville: Your First Adventure (Running the Game Ep 1)
tasks.prompt: Watch Colville's first Running the Game episode. Note how he frames the GM's role as designer and facilitator. Write down 3 design principles he implicitly demonstrates in his dungeon example.
tasks.output: 3 design principles extracted from Colville's approach.
checklist: Principles are about design, not just GMing technique.
Each principle references something specific from the video.

tasks.title: Play a one-page RPG: Honey Heist or Lasers & Feelings
tasks.prompt: Download and play Honey Heist or Lasers & Feelings (both are free/PWYW). While playing, take notes on: (1) how the resolution mechanic works, (2) how character creation functions, (3) what the rules do NOT cover and how players fill those gaps, (4) how the game creates a specific tone through mechanics alone.
tasks.output: Design analysis notes covering the 4 questions above.
checklist: Resolution mechanic is described precisely.
You identified at least 2 gaps the rules leave open.
You can explain how tone emerges from mechanics.

tasks.title: Essay: What makes RPGs distinct?
tasks.prompt: Write a 750-word essay defining what makes tabletop RPGs distinct from board games, video games, and freeform play. Reference Schell's lenses and Costikyan's vocabulary. Address: the role of the GM, shared imagined space, the lumpley principle (system as means of agreeing on fictional events), and how RPGs combine rules with open-ended fiction.
tasks.output: 750-word essay in your external workspace.
checklist: Definition is specific to TTRPGs, not games in general.
At least 2 Schell lenses and 2 Costikyan terms are used.
The lumpley principle or shared imagined space concept is addressed.
Essay is approximately 750 words.

weeklySchedule.topic: History and Evolution of RPGs

tasks.title: RPG Studies: History of Tabletop RPGs
tasks.prompt: Read the history chapters from Zagal & Deterding's Role-Playing Game Studies (White et al., 'Tabletop Role-Playing Games' chapter, and any chapters on wargaming precursors and the rise of D&D). Trace the evolution from wargames to OD&D to modern indie games. Note 3 turning points where design philosophy shifted.
tasks.output: Timeline notes with 3 identified design philosophy turning points.
checklist: Timeline covers wargaming roots through indie revolution.
Each turning point explains what changed in design philosophy.
At least one turning point is post-2000 (indie/Forge era).

tasks.title: The Forge: Big Model and Creative Agendas
tasks.prompt: Read the Forge Provisional Glossary. Focus on: the Big Model (Social Contract, Exploration, Shared Imagined Space, Creative Agenda, Techniques, Ephemera), the Lumpley Principle, and the three Creative Agendas (Gamism, Narrativism, Simulationism). Write a one-paragraph summary of each Creative Agenda with an example RPG that exemplifies it.
tasks.output: 3 Creative Agenda summaries with game examples.
checklist: All three Creative Agendas are defined in your own words.
Each has a specific game example.
You can explain the Lumpley Principle in one sentence.

tasks.title: Colville: Worldbuilding and Campaign Pitching
tasks.prompt: Watch Colville's worldbuilding and campaign pitching videos (Running the Game series). Note how he frames campaign design as setting player expectations. Write down his key sliders (levity, rating, weirdness, character focus) and think about how these apply to RPG design, not just GM prep.
tasks.output: Notes on Colville's campaign pitch framework.
checklist: All key sliders are listed.
You connected at least one slider to a design implication.
You can explain why pitching matters for game design.

tasks.title: Analysis: 3 RPGs from 3 eras
tasks.prompt: Pick 3 RPGs from different eras (e.g., OD&D or a retro clone, a 90s/00s game like Vampire or GURPS, and a modern indie game like Apocalypse World or Mothership). For each, write 250 words on: what design problem it solved, what innovation it introduced, and what limitation it carried forward. Total ~750 words.
tasks.output: 750-word comparative analysis.
checklist: Each RPG is from a genuinely different era.
Design problems and innovations are specific, not vague.
You identify at least one limitation carried forward in each.

tasks.title: Play an OSR or retro clone game
tasks.prompt: Play a session of an OSR game (Knave, Old School Essentials, or similar). Focus on how the rules shape play: lethality, gold-as-XP, reaction rolls, random encounters. After playing, write 300 words on how the design philosophy differs from a modern game like D&D 5e. What does the OSR assume about the GM and players?
tasks.output: 300-word OSR vs modern comparison.
checklist: Comparison references specific mechanics, not just vibes.
You identify what the OSR assumes about player skill vs character skill.
At least one design assumption is named explicitly.

weeklySchedule.topic: Game Design Theory: Rules, Play, Culture

tasks.title: Salen & Zimmerman: Defining Games, the Magic Circle, Meaningful Play
tasks.prompt: Read Rules of Play Ch 1-7 (What Is This Book About, The Design Process, Meaningful Play, Design, Systems, Interactivity, Defining Games). Focus on: the concept of the magic circle, meaningful play as the core goal of design, and their 8 definitions of games. Note how each definition applies (or breaks) when applied to TTRPGs.
tasks.output: Notes on magic circle, meaningful play, and 8 game definitions with TTRPG annotations.
checklist: Magic circle concept is explained in TTRPG terms.
Meaningful play is defined in your own words.
At least 4 of the 8 definitions are annotated for TTRPGs.

tasks.title: Koster: What Games Are, What They Teach
tasks.prompt: Read Koster's Theory of Fun Ch 1-7. Focus on his core argument: games are about learning and mastering patterns, and fun is the feeling of mastering a new pattern. Note how this applies to TTRPGs: what patterns do players learn? What happens when a TTRPG stops teaching new patterns? Write 3 examples of pattern-mastery in RPGs you have played.
tasks.output: 3 examples of pattern-mastery in TTRPGs.
checklist: Each example references a specific game and a specific pattern.
You can explain what 'fun is mastering patterns' means in your own words.
At least one example addresses what happens when patterns are exhausted.

tasks.title: Vincent Baker: Revisiting GNS and System
tasks.prompt: Read Vincent Baker's blog post 'Revisiting GNS' on lumpley.games and his writings on the lumpley principle (system as means of agreeing on fictional events). Write a 250-word reflection: how does understanding system as credibility (not just rules) change how you think about RPG design? What does it mean for a rule to allocate credibility?
tasks.output: 250-word reflection on system as credibility.
tasks.documentName: W03 - Baker on system and credibility
checklist: Reflection references the lumpley principle specifically.
At least one example of a rule allocating credibility is given.
You distinguish between 'rules' and 'system' in Baker's terms.

tasks.title: Bowman: Indie TTRPG Design Basics
tasks.prompt: Watch Sarah Lynne Bowman's lecture on indie TTRPG design (part 1 or 2 of her series). Note how she connects the Forge discourse community to the indie RPG revolution. Write down 3 design principles from Fiasco or Apocalypse World that subvert traditional RPG design assumptions.
tasks.output: 3 subversive design principles from indie RPGs.
checklist: Each principle is about design, not just culture.
You explain what traditional assumption each principle subverts.
At least one principle is from Fiasco or Apocalypse World.

tasks.title: Analysis: Rules, Play, Culture schema applied to a TTRPG
tasks.prompt: Pick one TTRPG you know well. Analyze it using Salen & Zimmerman's three schemas: Rules (formal system, operational/constitutive/implicit rules), Play (experiential, what players actually do and feel), and Culture (social context, community norms, what the game says about its milieu). Write 250 words per schema, ~750 words total. Conclude with how the three schemas interact.
tasks.output: 750-word three-schema analysis.
checklist: All three schemas are addressed with equal depth.
Rules section distinguishes operational, constitutive, and implicit rules.
Culture section addresses community, not just setting.
The interaction conclusion is analytical, not summary.

weeklySchedule.topic: The Player Experience

tasks.title: Schell: The Player, the Mind, Motivation, Mechanics, Balance
tasks.prompt: Read Schell Ch 10-14 (The Game Is Made for a Player, The Experience Is in the Player's Mind, The Player's Mind Is Driven by Motivation, Some Elements Are Game Mechanics, Game Mechanics Must Be in Balance). Focus on: what motivates RPG players specifically, how mechanics create emotional responses, and what 'balance' means in a cooperative storytelling game. Note 3 lenses from these chapters that apply to TTRPG design.
tasks.output: Notes on player motivation, mechanics, and balance with 3 TTRPG-specific lenses.
checklist: Player motivation section addresses TTRPG-specific motivations.
Balance discussion addresses cooperative vs competitive dynamics.
3 lenses are specific and actionable.

tasks.title: Tabletop: Analog Game Design - selected essays
tasks.prompt: Read 2-3 essays from Costikyan & Davidson's Tabletop: Analog Game Design (available free online). Focus on essays about game balance, player interaction, or game structures. Write 300 words on how the essayists' principles apply to TTRPGs, which are analog games with a human referee.
tasks.output: 300-word essay application notes.
checklist: At least 2 specific essays are referenced by author and topic.
Application to TTRPGs is explicit, not implied.
You note at least one principle that works differently with a human referee.

tasks.title: RPG PHD: Dieter Rams' Ten Principles applied to TTRPGs
tasks.prompt: Watch RPG PHD's video applying Dieter Rams' Ten Principles of Good Design to tabletop RPG mechanics. For each principle, write one sentence evaluating a TTRPG you know. Which principles does your favorite game violate, and does that matter?
tasks.output: 10 principle evaluations (one sentence each).
checklist: All 10 principles are addressed.
Each evaluation references a specific game.
At least one violation is identified and discussed.

tasks.title: Play/read Mork Borg Bare Bones Edition
tasks.prompt: Download and read Mork Borg Bare Bones Edition (free). Play a short session if possible. Analyze how the game's tone (bleak, apocalyptic, black metal) is embedded in the rules themselves, not just the art. Write 300 words on what specific mechanics create the game's emotional register.
tasks.output: 300-word analysis of tone through mechanics.
checklist: Analysis identifies specific mechanics, not just descriptions.
At least 2 mechanics are linked to specific emotional effects.
You address how rules without art still convey tone.

tasks.title: Player experience analysis with interviews
tasks.prompt: Interview 2-3 RPG players about what they enjoy most in TTRPGs. Ask: what was your best session and why? What mechanics do you love or hate? What do you want from a session that you rarely get? Map their answers to Schell's motivation framework (Ch 12) and Koster's theory of fun. Write 750 words analyzing what your interviews reveal about player experience design.
tasks.output: 750-word player experience analysis.
checklist: At least 2 players are interviewed.
Schell's motivation framework is explicitly applied.
Koster's theory of fun is explicitly applied.
You identify at least one design insight from the interviews.

weeklySchedule.topic: Resolution Mechanics and Probability

tasks.title: Schell: Mechanics and Balance (revisited)
tasks.prompt: Re-read Schell Ch 13-15 (Game Mechanics, Game Mechanics Must Be in Balance, Game Mechanics Support Puzzles). Focus on: how mechanics create different types of player experiences, what balance means for different game types, and how mechanics can support or undermine player agency. Write notes specifically on how these apply to dice resolution systems.
tasks.output: Notes on mechanics, balance, and puzzles applied to resolution systems.
checklist: Notes address dice resolution specifically.
Balance is discussed in terms of probability and player experience.
At least one lens is applied to a specific resolution mechanic.

tasks.title: Fullerton: Formal Elements and Balance
tasks.prompt: Read Fullerton Game Design Workshop Ch 3 (Working with Formal Elements) and Ch 10 (Functionality, Completeness, and Balance). Focus on: how formal elements (rules, resources, boundaries, outcomes) map to TTRPG resolution systems, and Fullerton's methods for testing balance. Note 3 balance-testing techniques you could apply to an RPG.
tasks.output: Notes on formal elements + 3 balance-testing techniques.
checklist: Formal elements are mapped to TTRPG-specific examples.
3 balance-testing techniques are described concretely.
You can explain the difference between functional, complete, and balanced.

tasks.title: Colville: Combat and encounter design
tasks.prompt: Watch Colville's Running the Game episode on combat design or encounter building. Note how he thinks about difficulty, player agency, and mechanical transparency. Write 200 words on how encounter design principles translate to resolution mechanic design.
tasks.output: 200-word encounter-to-resolution translation notes.
checklist: Translation addresses player agency specifically.
At least one Colville principle is applied to resolution design.

tasks.title: Compare resolution in 3 systems
tasks.prompt: Create the same basic character in 3 systems with different resolution approaches: D&D 5e (d20 + modifier vs DC), Apocalypse World or a PbtA hack (2d6 + stat, 7-9 partial success), and Mothership (d100 roll-under). Attempt the same task in each (e.g., climbing a wall, intimidating a guard). Document: how does the probability feel? What information does the player have? How does failure push the fiction forward (or not)?
tasks.output: Comparative resolution analysis with probability notes.
checklist: All 3 systems are compared on the same task.
Probability is noted for each (not just vibes).
You address how failure affects the fiction in each system.

tasks.title: Design a core resolution mechanic
tasks.prompt: Design an original core resolution mechanic for a TTRPG. Specify: dice type and number, what players roll vs what the GM rolls (if anything), success/failure thresholds, how difficulty is modulated, and what happens on partial success. Calculate the probability of success at 3 difficulty levels for a baseline character. Write 500 words including the probability table and a design rationale explaining why this mechanic creates the experience you want.
tasks.output: 500-word mechanic document with probability table and rationale.
checklist: Mechanic is fully specified (dice, thresholds, difficulty).
Probability table covers at least 3 difficulty levels.
Rationale connects the mechanic to a desired player experience.
Partial success or complication mechanics are addressed (if applicable).

weeklySchedule.topic: Character Design and Progression

tasks.title: Schell: Characters and Spaces
tasks.prompt: Read Schell Ch 21-22 (Worlds Contain Characters, Worlds Contain Spaces). Focus on how character design in games differs from character design in fiction: game characters are tools for player expression. Note 3 lenses from these chapters that apply to TTRPG character creation and progression.
tasks.output: Notes on game character design + 3 TTRPG-specific lenses.
checklist: Distinction between game characters and fiction characters is noted.
3 lenses are specific to TTRPG character creation.
Progression is addressed as a design problem.

tasks.title: Fullerton: Dramatic Elements
tasks.prompt: Read Fullerton Ch 4 (Working with Dramatic Elements). Focus on: character as a dramatic element, story structures, and how dramatic elements interact with formal systems. Write 300 words on how TTRPG character sheets function as both formal (rules) and dramatic (story) elements simultaneously.
tasks.output: 300-word analysis of character sheets as formal + dramatic elements.
checklist: Analysis references specific character sheet elements.
Formal and dramatic functions of the same element are both addressed.
At least one example from a real game is used.

tasks.title: The Alexandrian: System design and pitfalls
tasks.prompt: Read Justin Alexander's essays on system design and common pitfalls (search the Alexandrian for 'system design' or 'design pitfalls'). Note 3 specific design pitfalls he identifies and how they apply to character systems. Write 200 words on how these pitfalls manifest in games you have played.
tasks.output: 200-word notes on 3 system design pitfalls.
checklist: 3 specific pitfalls are named.
Each pitfall is connected to character design.
At least one pitfall is illustrated from personal play experience.

tasks.title: Character creation in 3 different RPGs
tasks.prompt: Create 2 characters each in 3 RPGs with different character design philosophies (e.g., class-based like D&D, playbook-based like PbtA, skill-based like Call of Cthulhu or GURPS). For each system, note: what choices the player makes, what the system decides for the player, how long creation takes, and what the character sheet tells you about what the game values.
tasks.output: Comparative character creation analysis (3 systems, 6 characters).
checklist: All 3 systems are compared on the same axes.
You identify what each system values based on sheet design.
Time to create is noted for each.

tasks.title: Design a character creation system
tasks.prompt: Design a character creation system for the RPG you started building in Week 5. Include: 3-4 archetypes or classes (or an alternative structure), 4-6 key attributes or skills, a resource pool (HP, willpower, luck, etc.), and a progression mechanic (how characters improve). Write 1000 words or equivalent in rules text format. Include a sample completed character sheet.
tasks.output: 1000-word character system document + sample character sheet.
checklist: System includes all required elements (archetypes, attributes, resources, progression).
Rules text is written as if for a player, not as design notes.
Sample character sheet is complete and usable.
Progression mechanic is specified, not just implied.

weeklySchedule.topic: Combat, Conflict, and Tension

tasks.title: Schell: Interest Curves and Balance
tasks.prompt: Read Schell Ch 17 (Experiences Can Be Judged by Their Interest Curves) and revisit Ch 14 (Game Mechanics Must Be in Balance) with combat in mind. Focus on: how interest curves apply to combat pacing (rising tension, climax, resolution), and what balance means in combat where one side is the GM. Write notes on how to design combat that follows an interest curve rather than a flat difficulty line.
tasks.output: Notes on interest curves in combat + balance with a GM opponent.
tasks.documentName: W07 - Schell tension and interest curves
checklist: Interest curve concept is applied to combat pacing specifically.
Balance with a GM opponent is addressed (GM is not trying to win).
At least one example of good combat pacing is analyzed.

tasks.title: Fullerton: System Dynamics and Feedback Loops
tasks.prompt: Read Fullerton Ch 5 (Working with System Dynamics). Focus on: feedback loops (positive and negative), emergent systems, and how dynamic systems create unexpected interactions. Write 300 words identifying feedback loops in a TTRPG combat system you know well. Which loops create escalating tension? Which create death spirals?
tasks.output: 300-word feedback loop analysis of a combat system.
checklist: At least 2 feedback loops are identified (one positive, one negative).
Death spirals are addressed if present.
Analysis references a specific game's combat system.

tasks.title: RPG PHD: Combat pacing and cognitive load
tasks.prompt: Watch an RPG PHD video on combat pacing, cognitive load, or mechanic clarity (browse the channel for relevant content). Note 3 specific principles for reducing cognitive load in combat while maintaining tactical depth. Write 200 words on how these principles apply to your in-progress RPG.
tasks.output: 200-word cognitive load analysis for your RPG's combat.
checklist: 3 principles are specific and actionable.
Application to your own RPG is concrete.
You address the tension between depth and cognitive load.

tasks.title: Run the same combat in 2 systems
tasks.prompt: Design a simple combat scenario (a bandit ambush in a forest clearing). Run it (or play it) in 2 systems: one traditional (D&D, Pathfinder, or similar) and one narrative (PbtA, Forged in the Dark, or similar). Document: how long each combat takes, where the tension peaks, what choices players make, and how failure drives the story. Write 400 words comparing the two experiences.
tasks.output: 400-word comparative combat analysis.
checklist: Same scenario is used for both systems.
Time, tension, and player choices are compared.
You identify how each system's combat creates (or fails to create) an interest curve.

tasks.title: Design a conflict resolution system
tasks.prompt: Design a complete conflict resolution system for your RPG. Choose an approach: HP-based, clock/progress tracker, stakes-based, threat tokens, or a hybrid. Write the complete rules text for resolving a physical combat and a social conflict. Include: how conflicts start, how actions are resolved, how consequences escalate, and how conflicts end. 1000 words.
tasks.output: 1000-word conflict resolution rules document.
checklist: Both physical and social conflicts are addressed.
Escalation mechanics are specified.
Rules text is written for players, not as design notes.
The system integrates with your resolution mechanic from Week 5.

weeklySchedule.topic: The GM Role and Game Structure

tasks.title: The Alexandrian: Node-based scenario design
tasks.prompt: Read Justin Alexander's node-based scenario design series (Parts 1-5) and 'Using Revelation Lists' from the Alexandrian. Focus on: how nodes connect through clues, the difference between linear, branching, and node-based structures, and how revelation lists track what information players have. Write notes on why node-based design works for RPGs where player agency is paramount.
tasks.output: Notes on node-based design with 3 key principles extracted.
checklist: All 5 parts of the series are read.
3 key principles are extracted and stated clearly.
You can explain the difference between linear, branching, and node structures.

tasks.title: Colville: Prepping adventures and campaign structure
tasks.prompt: Watch Colville's Running the Game episodes on prepping adventures and campaign structure. Note how he organizes information for the GM (annotated maps, bullet-point notes, key NPCs). Write 300 words on what makes good GM-facing design: how should rules and scenarios present information to the person running the game?
tasks.output: 300-word GM-facing design principles.
checklist: Notes address information organization for GMs.
At least 3 GM-facing design principles are identified.
Principles are about design, not just prep technique.

tasks.title: Design a node-based one-shot scenario
tasks.prompt: Design a one-shot scenario for your RPG using node-based design. Include: 5-7 nodes (locations, NPCs, or events), clue links connecting each node to at least 2 others, a revelation list, and at least 3 paths to the conclusion. Create a visual scenario map showing the node structure. Write 500-750 words of scenario content plus the map.
tasks.output: Scenario document with node map, clue links, and revelation list.
checklist: 5-7 nodes are present and connected.
Each node has at least 2 clue links to other nodes.
Revelation list is included.
At least 3 paths to the conclusion are possible.
Scenario uses your RPG's mechanics (resolution, character, conflict).

tasks.title: GM a session using your scenario
tasks.prompt: Run your node-based scenario for at least 2 players using your RPG's mechanics. After the session, write 300 words on: (1) which nodes did players reach, and which did they skip? (2) Did the clue links work or did players get stuck? (3) Where did your mechanics support the scenario, and where did they fight it? (4) What would you revise?
tasks.output: 300-word GM session report with revision notes.
checklist: Report addresses all 4 questions.
At least one mechanical issue is identified.
At least one revision is specified.

weeklySchedule.topic: Setting and Worldbuilding

tasks.title: Schell: Worlds, Characters, Spaces, Aesthetics
tasks.prompt: Read Schell Ch 20-23 (Stories and Games Take Place in Worlds, Worlds Contain Characters, Worlds Contain Spaces, The Look and Feel of a World Is Defined by Its Aesthetics). Focus on: what makes a game world different from a novel world (it must be playable), how spaces create gameplay, and how aesthetics communicate tone. Note 3 lenses for TTRPG setting design.
tasks.output: Notes on game worlds + 3 TTRPG setting lenses.
checklist: Distinction between game worlds and fiction worlds is noted.
3 lenses are specific to TTRPG setting design.
Aesthetics is discussed in terms of rules text, not just art.

tasks.title: Fullerton: Dramatic elements revisited + accessibility
tasks.prompt: Re-read Fullerton Ch 4 (dramatic elements) with setting design in mind, and read Ch 11 (Fun and Accessibility). Focus on: how setting functions as a dramatic element, and how to make your setting accessible to new players (what to explain, what to leave for discovery). Write 300 words on what makes a TTRPG setting 'immediately playable.'
tasks.output: 300-word analysis of playable settings.
checklist: Accessibility is addressed for new players.
You distinguish between what to explain upfront vs discover in play.
At least one example of an immediately playable setting is analyzed.

tasks.title: Colville: Worldbuilding
tasks.prompt: Watch Colville's worldbuilding videos from the Running the Game series. Note his approach: start small, build outward, let play demand detail. Write 200 words on how his 'bottom-up' worldbuilding differs from top-down worldbuilding, and which approach serves TTRPG design better.
tasks.output: 200-word bottom-up vs top-down worldbuilding analysis.
checklist: Distinction between approaches is clear.
You argue for which approach serves TTRPGs better and why.
At least one practical example is given.

tasks.title: Deconstruct 3 one-page RPG settings
tasks.prompt: Find and read 3 one-page RPGs or micro-settings on itch.io (search 'one-page RPG' or 'micro setting'). For each, deconstruct: what tone is established in the first sentence? What is the core conflict? How many factions or NPCs are defined? How much is left open for the GM? Write 100 words per setting.
tasks.output: 3 setting deconstructions (100 words each).
checklist: 3 settings are deconstructed on the same axes.
You identify what each setting leaves open vs defines.
At least one setting's tone is traced to specific word choices.

tasks.title: Create a one-page setting document
tasks.prompt: Create a one-page setting document for your in-progress RPG. Include: a 2-sentence tone statement, the core conflict that drives adventures, 3 factions with competing interests, 1 key location with a map sketch, and 3 adventure hooks. The document should be immediately playable: a GM should be able to run a session from it without additional material.
tasks.output: One-page setting document (ready to play).
checklist: Tone statement is 2 sentences and evocative.
Core conflict is specific and actionable.
3 factions have competing (not just different) interests.
At least 3 adventure hooks are included.
A GM could run a session from this document alone.

weeklySchedule.topic: Adventure and Scenario Design

tasks.title: The Alexandrian: Pacing, Three Clue Rule, scenario structure
tasks.prompt: Read Justin Alexander's essays: 'The Art of Pacing,' 'The Three Clue Rule,' and any scenario structure essays on the Alexandrian. Focus on: how pacing works in RPGs (it is not the GM's job to control pacing, but to create structures that produce good pacing), and why 3 clues per revelation is the minimum. Write notes on how these principles refine your Week 8 node-based design.
tasks.output: Notes on pacing and Three Clue Rule with refinements to Week 8 design.
checklist: Three Clue Rule is explained with an example.
Pacing essay principles are applied to your Week 8 scenario.
At least one refinement to your earlier design is noted.

tasks.title: Fullerton: Ideation and prototyping for adventures
tasks.prompt: Read Fullerton Ch 6 (Ideation) and Ch 7 (Prototyping). Adapt these to adventure design: how do you prototype an adventure? What does iteration look like for a scenario? Write 300 words on how Fullerton's prototyping methods apply to RPG adventure design, where the 'prototype' is a set of notes and the 'test' is running it for players.
tasks.output: 300-word prototyping methods for adventures.
checklist: Prototyping is adapted to adventure design specifically.
Iteration cycle for scenarios is described.
At least one prototyping technique from Fullerton is applied.

tasks.title: Design a complete one-shot adventure
tasks.prompt: Design a complete one-shot adventure for your RPG. Include: scenario structure (node-based or other), 5-7 encounters or scenes, 3-5 NPCs with motivations, at least 2 resolution paths, and a revelation list. Integrate your setting from Week 9. Write 1500 words or equivalent in adventure format (not design notes, but playable content).
tasks.output: 1500-word playable adventure document.
checklist: Adventure is playable, not just outlined.
At least 2 resolution paths are possible.
NPCs have motivations, not just stats.
Revelation list is included.
Adventure integrates your setting and mechanics.

tasks.title: Run your adventure for players
tasks.prompt: Run your one-shot adventure for at least 2 players. After the session, write 400 words on: (1) Did players follow any of your expected paths? (2) Where did the Three Clue Rule hold or fail? (3) Which encounters created the most tension? (4) What would you cut, add, or revise? This playtest report feeds directly into your final project.
tasks.output: 400-word adventure playtest report.
checklist: All 4 questions are addressed.
Three Clue Rule is evaluated explicitly.
At least 3 specific revisions are identified.
Report connects to what needs fixing in your final project.

weeklySchedule.topic: Narrative Mechanics and Story Games

tasks.title: Schell: Story and game structures, indirect control
tasks.prompt: Read Schell Ch 18-19 (One Kind of Experience Is the Story, Story and Game Structures Can Be Artfully Merged with Indirect Control). Focus on: the fundamental conflict between story (predetermined) and game (open-ended), and Schell's concept of indirect control (designing structures that guide players toward satisfying outcomes without forcing them). Write notes on how indirect control applies to TTRPG design.
tasks.output: Notes on story/game conflict + indirect control in TTRPGs.

title: LGST 201: Basics of Criminal Law
subject: Legal Studies
description: An introductory survey of American criminal law, covering the sources and structure of criminal law, constitutional protections, the elements of a crime, defenses, parties to crime, inchoate offenses, and major categories of criminal offenses including homicide, property crimes, and crimes against the public. Designed for undergraduates and self-study learners with no prior legal background.
objectives: Identify the sources of American criminal law and distinguish criminal law from civil law.
Explain the constitutional protections that govern the criminal justice system, including key Bill of Rights provisions.
Analyze the elements of a crime: actus reus, mens rea, causation, and concurrence.
Evaluate criminal defenses including self-defense, necessity, duress, insanity, and intoxication.
Distinguish between principals, accomplices, and accessories in party liability.
Classify inchoate offenses: attempt, conspiracy, and solicitation.
Differentiate categories of criminal homicide: murder, manslaughter, and their degrees.
Identify elements of property crimes, public order crimes, and crimes against the government.
Apply criminal law concepts to hypothetical fact patterns and case analyses.
Articulate theories of punishment and their implications for criminal justice policy.

resources.label: Introduction to Criminal Law (Open Textbook Library)
resources.note: Free open-access textbook by University of Minnesota Libraries Publishing. 13 chapters covering the full scope of undergraduate criminal law. CC BY-NC-SA license.

resources.label: The Law Academy: Introduction to Criminal Law (YouTube)
resources.note: YouTube playlist covering intro to criminal law, theories, punishment, types of crime, actus reus, mens rea, defenses, homicide, and more. ~10 min per video.

resources.label: Studicata: Criminal Law Crash Course (YouTube)
resources.note: 19 longer videos explaining criminal law elements, offenses, and defenses. Law school and bar exam prep level, useful for deeper understanding.

resources.label: Cornell LII: Criminal Law (Wex Legal Encyclopedia)
resources.note: Free legal dictionary and encyclopedia entry on criminal law. Overview of types of crimes, categories, and key concepts. Good reference throughout the course.

resources.label: Oyez: US Supreme Court Cases
resources.note: Free archive of Supreme Court case audio, transcripts, and summaries. Use for researching constitutional criminal procedure cases.

resources.label: Coursera: An Introduction to American Law (Criminal Law module)
resources.note: Free to audit. Includes a criminal law module from University of Pennsylvania Law School. Good supplementary video lectures.

title: LGST 101: Basics of Corporate Law
subject: Legal Studies
description: An introductory survey of corporate law covering the legal environment of business, agency relationships, partnerships, corporate formation and governance, fiduciary duties, securities regulation, and contemporary debates about corporate purpose. Designed for students with no prior legal background.
objectives: Identify the sources of American law and the structure of the US legal system as it applies to business entities.
Explain the principal-agent relationship and describe the duties and liabilities that arise from agency.
Distinguish among sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited liability companies, and corporations.
Describe the process of corporate formation, including filing requirements and the concept of separate legal personality.
Analyze the doctrine of limited liability and the circumstances under which courts may pierce the corporate veil.
Explain the fiduciary duties of corporate directors and officers, including duty of care, duty of loyalty, and the business judgment rule.
Describe the basics of corporate finance, including stocks, bonds, dividends, and initial public offerings.
Evaluate competing theories of corporate purpose, including shareholder primacy and stakeholder governance.

title: LIBR 201: Information Architecture
subject: Library Science
description: An intermediate introduction to information architecture: the theory and practice of organizing digital information so it is findable, navigable, and understandable. Covers organization systems, labeling, navigation, search, metadata, controlled vocabularies, user research methods (card sorting, tree testing, content audits), IA strategy, and the ethical design of information environments. Includes a semester-long applied IA project on a real website or system.
objectives: Define information architecture and explain the problems it addresses in digital environments.
Analyze and evaluate the organization, labeling, navigation, and search systems of an existing website.
Apply user research methods including content audits, card sorting, and tree testing to inform IA decisions.
Design and document an IA strategy including sitemaps, wireframes, and taxonomy structures.
Understand the role of metadata, controlled vocabularies, and thesauri in supporting findability.
Evaluate the ethical dimensions of information architecture and its impact on users and society.
Produce a complete IA project from research through strategy to design documentation and presentation.

resources.label: Rosenfeld, Morville & Arango, Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (4th Ed, O'Reilly 2015)
resources.note: Primary textbook. The canonical 'polar bear' book. Covers organization, labeling, navigation, search, metadata, research, strategy, and design.

resources.label: Abby Covert, How to Make Sense of Any Mess: Information Architecture for Everybody (2014)
resources.note: Practical seven-step process for making sense of any information mess. Accessible, workbook-style. Used at UT Austin iSchool.

resources.label: Lisa Maria Martin, Everyday Information Architecture (A Book Apart, 2019)
resources.note: Compact guide to applying IA principles in everyday digital work. Covers content analysis, taxonomy, and structure.

resources.label: Steve Krug, Don't Make Me Think, Revisited (3rd Ed, New Riders 2014)
resources.note: Classic web usability companion. Covers intuitive navigation, information design, and usability testing on a budget.

resources.label: Jorge Arango, Living in Information: Responsible Design for Digital Places (Rosenfeld Media, 2019)
resources.note: Explores IA through the lens of physical architecture. Covers ethical design of information environments, attention, and social impact.

resources.label: Donna Spencer, A Practical Guide to Information Architecture (2nd Ed, UX Mastery)
resources.note: Free PDF. Practical guide covering content organization, labeling, navigation, and IA project process. Great supplementary reference.

resources.label: NN/g Information Architecture Study Guide
resources.note: Free collection of articles and videos on card sorting, tree testing, navigation design, and IA research methods from Nielsen Norman Group.

resources.label: Optimal Workshop (OptimalSort, Treejack)
resources.note: Free tier available. Industry-standard tools for card sorting and tree testing. Used for the applied project.

resources.label: Information Architecture Guide for UX Designers (YouTube)
resources.note: Short overview video covering what IA is, why it matters, navigation, elements of IA, and how to design it.

resources.label: Information Architecture: From Chaos to Clarity (YouTube)
resources.note: Video covering the IA process from understanding users to organizing content and testing structures.

resources.label: A Beginner's Guide to Information Architecture (YouTube)
resources.note: 8-minute beginner-friendly introduction to IA concepts and principles.
