title: ECON 260: Behavioral Economics
subject: Economics
description: An intermediate survey of behavioral economics, tracing the field from Herbert Simon's bounded rationality through Kahneman and Tversky's heuristics-and-biases program, prospect theory, intertemporal choice, social preferences, and Thaler and Sunstein's nudge theory. Students engage with primary sources, classic experiments, and real-world applications in finance, public policy, and everyday decision-making.
objectives: Explain the historical emergence of behavioral economics and its challenge to the rational-actor model.
Identify and apply key heuristics (availability, representativeness, anchoring) and their associated biases.
Compare prospect theory to expected utility theory, explaining loss aversion, reference dependence, and probability weighting.
Analyze intertemporal choice problems including present bias, hyperbolic discounting, and self-control strategies.
Evaluate the role of social preferences (fairness, reciprocity, conformity) in economic decision-making.
Apply nudge theory and choice architecture principles to real-world policy and business problems.
Critically assess the ethics of libertarian paternalism and common critiques of behavioral economics.
Design a behavioral intervention for a self-selected problem and evaluate its expected effectiveness.

resources.label: Arthur Caplan, A Practicum in Behavioral Economics (CC BY 4.0)
resources.note: Free open-access textbook. Primary reference for the course. Organized in four sections: irrational quirks, Homo economicus vs. Homo sapiens, behavioral game theory, and empirical studies.

resources.label: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow
resources.note: Core trade book. Kahneman's magisterial overview of System 1/System 2, heuristics, prospect theory, and overconfidence. Available at any library or bookstore.

resources.label: Richard Thaler, Misbehaving: The Making of Behavioral Economics
resources.note: Core trade book. Thaler's personal history of the field, from mental accounting through nudge theory. Accessible and often funny.

resources.label: Dan Ariely, Predictably Irrational
resources.note: Supplementary trade book. Ariely's engaging introduction to behavioral economics through experiments on cheating, pricing, and self-control.

resources.label: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, Nudge
resources.note: Core trade book for the policy section. The foundational text on choice architecture and libertarian paternalism.

resources.label: Kahneman and Tversky, Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk (1979)
resources.note: The foundational paper. Econometrica, 47(2), 263-291. Free PDF.

resources.label: Tversky and Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974)
resources.note: The seminal Science paper introducing representativeness, availability, and anchoring. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131.

resources.label: Dan Ariely, A Beginner's Guide to Irrational Behavior (free course archive)
resources.note: Free archived online course from Duke. Six weeks of video lectures covering visual illusions, cheating, self-control, motivation, and emotion.

resources.label: MIT OpenCourseWare 14.13: Psychology and Economics (Spring 2020)
resources.note: Free course materials including lecture videos, lecture notes, problem sets, and exams from Prof. Frank Schilbach.

resources.label: Thaler and Sunstein, Nudge Chapter 1 (free PDF)
resources.note: Free excerpt: Introduction and Chapter 1 (Biases and Blunders). Covers System 1/System 2, anchoring, loss aversion, and status quo bias.

resources.label: Thaler, Sunstein, and Balz, Choice Architecture (free PDF)
resources.note: Academic paper on the tools of choice architecture: defaults, expecting error, understanding mappings, giving feedback, structuring complex choices, and incentives.

title: IDST 201: Systems Thinking
subject: Interdisciplinary Studies
description: A mixed-theory-and-practice introduction to systems thinking, the discipline of seeing wholes rather than parts. Drawn from engineering, ecology, management, and social science, the course covers feedback loops, stocks and flows, system archetypes, leverage points, and system dynamics modeling. Apply these tools to real-world problems from organizational design to sustainability.
objectives: Define a system and distinguish systems thinking from reductionist analysis.
Identify stocks, flows, and feedback loops (balancing and reinforcing) in real-world systems.
Construct causal loop diagrams to map system structure and behavior.
Recognize and diagnose common system archetypes (success to the successful, shifting the burden, fixes that fail, etc.).
Apply Donella Meadows's leverage points framework to identify high-leverage interventions.
Build and simulate a basic system dynamics model using Vensim PLE.
Evaluate systems thinking approaches in organizational, ecological, and social contexts.
Synthesize systems thinking principles into a final analysis of a self-selected complex problem.

resources.label: Meadows, Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)
resources.note: Primary textbook. Chelsea Green Publishing. The classic concise primer by Donella Meadows.

resources.label: Senge, The Fifth Discipline (1990/2006)
resources.note: Secondary textbook. Currency/Doubleday. Systems thinking applied to learning organizations.

resources.label: Cabrera & Cabrera, Systems Thinking Made Simple (2018)
resources.note: Supplementary text. DSRP framework (Distinctions, Systems, Relationships, Perspectives). Used at Cornell and West Point.

resources.label: Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)
resources.note: Free online essay. The most-accessed resource in the Donella Meadows archive. Required reading.

resources.label: Ramage & Shipp, Systems Thinkers (Springer, 2009)
resources.note: Reference library. Biographical history of 30 major systems thinkers with excerpts from their writing.

resources.label: Sterman, All Models Are Wrong: Reflections on Becoming a Systems Scientist (2002)
resources.note: Free via MIT DSpace. System Dynamics Review, 18(4), 501-531.

resources.label: Ackoff on Systems Thinking and Management (2003 lecture)
resources.note: Russell Ackoff's classic presentation. Analysis vs. synthesis, why a system is never the sum of its parts.

resources.label: Vensim PLE (free system dynamics software)
resources.note: Free for personal and educational use. Download and install for the modeling units.

resources.label: The Donella Meadows Project
resources.note: Reference library. Archive of Meadows's columns, essays, and systems thinking resources.

resources.label: Wheatley, Leadership and the New Science (3rd ed, 2006)
resources.note: Reference library. New science perspectives on organizations as living systems.

weeklySchedule.topic: System resilience, self-organization, and hierarchy

weeklySchedule.topic: Leverage points: places to intervene in a system

title: PHIL 210: Albert Camus, Absurdism and Revolt
subject: Philosophy
description: A six-week mini course on the philosophy of Albert Camus, tracing the arc from absurdism in The Myth of Sisyphus through the literary expression of the absurd in The Stranger, to collective revolt and political ethics in The Plague and Neither Victims nor Executioners. Read Camus in his own words and engage with his central questions: Why should I not kill myself? Why should I not kill others? What does it mean to live without appeal?
objectives: Explain what Camus means by 'the absurd' and how it differs from nihilism and existentialism.
Reconstruct Camus's argument against suicide in The Myth of Sisyphus and evaluate its soundness.
Interpret The Stranger as a literary enactment of absurd consciousness, identifying key philosophical moments.
Trace the development from individual absurd revolt to collective political revolt in The Plague.
Articulate Camus's ethic of 'neither victims nor executioners' and assess its relevance to contemporary political violence.
Compare Camus's rejection of systematic philosophy with Sartrean existentialism and assess the Camus-Sartre split.
Defend your own position on whether Camus's response to the absurd is livable, with textual evidence.

weeklySchedule.topic: Who was Camus and what is the absurd?

tasks.title: SEP entry on Albert Camus (sections 1-3)
tasks.prompt: Read sections 1 through 3 of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Camus. Take notes on: (1) the paradoxes of Camus's absurdist philosophy, (2) what Camus means by 'the absurd', and (3) how the SEP distinguishes Camus from existentialism. Write down two questions you have after reading.
tasks.output: Notes with definitions, distinctions, and two questions.
checklist: Defined 'the absurd' in your own words.
Identified at least one difference between Camus and Sartre.
Noted two genuine questions raised by the reading.

tasks.title: Absurdism, Rebellion and The Art of Living (first 45 min)
tasks.prompt: Watch the first 45 minutes of this overview. Note how the narrator frames the absurd as a collision between human need for meaning and the universe's silence. Write one paragraph comparing this framing to what you read in the SEP entry.
tasks.output: One paragraph comparing the video framing to the SEP entry.
checklist: Identified the core definition of the absurd from the video.
Compared it explicitly to the SEP entry.
Noted at least one point of disagreement or nuance.

tasks.title: Reading response 1: What is the absurd?
tasks.prompt: In approximately 300 words, answer: What does Camus mean by 'the absurd', and why does he insist it is neither a property of the world alone nor of human thought alone? Use at least one quotation from the SEP entry to ground your answer. End with one objection or question of your own.
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Defined the absurd as a relationship, not a thing.
Used at least one quotation with attribution.
Raised one objection or question.
Word count is approximately 300 words.

weeklySchedule.topic: The Myth of Sisyphus: suicide and the absurd response

tasks.title: The Myth of Sisyphus, chapters 1-2 (An Absurd Reasoning, The Absurd Man)
tasks.prompt: Read the opening chapters of The Myth of Sisyphus. Camus opens: 'There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.' Trace his argument: why does the absurd not warrant suicide? Identify the three consequences Camus draws from absurd consciousness (revolt, freedom, passion). Note passages where he rejects 'philosophical suicide' (leaping to God or hope).
tasks.output: Notes tracing the argument structure, with three key passages quoted.
checklist: Identified Camus's opening claim and its role in the argument.
Listed the three consequences of absurd consciousness.
Quoted at least three passages with page references.
Defined 'philosophical suicide' in your own words.

tasks.title: Philosophy Core Concepts: Camus on Belief, Truth, and Action
tasks.prompt: Watch this focused lecture on the relationship between the absurd and action. Note how the lecturer explains Camus's rejection of both faith and nihilism. Write down one point where the lecture clarified something confusing in your reading.
tasks.output: One paragraph noting a clarification from the lecture.
checklist: Identified one specific clarification the lecture provided.
Connected the lecture point to a specific passage in the reading.

tasks.title: Reading response 2: Is Camus's argument against suicide sound?
tasks.prompt: In approximately 350 words, reconstruct Camus's argument against suicide in your own words. Then raise one objection: is there a gap in his reasoning? Does accepting the absurd truly entail continuing to live? Consider whether someone might accept the absurd and still find life not worth continuing. Reference at least one passage from the reading.
tasks.output: ~350 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Reconstructed the argument fairly, step by step.
Raised a specific, charitable objection.
Referenced at least one passage.
Word count is approximately 350 words.

weeklySchedule.topic: The Myth of Sisyphus: Sisyphus happy, and the absurd creation

tasks.title: The Myth of Sisyphus, chapter 4 (The Myth of Sisyphus) and chapter 3 (Absurd Creation)
tasks.prompt: Read the final chapter (the Sisyphus myth itself) and the chapter on absurd creation. Focus on the famous line: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' Why must we imagine this? How does Camus connect the figure of Sisyphus to the absurd man? In the creation chapter, note how Camus treats art and literature as a response to the absurd.
tasks.output: Notes on the Sisyphus conclusion and absurd creation, with two key quotations.
checklist: Explained why Camus says we must imagine Sisyphus happy.
Connected Sisyphus to at least one earlier figure (Don Juan, actor, conqueror).
Quoted two passages with page references.
Noted how art functions as an absurd response.

tasks.title: The Myth of Sisyphus audiobook (final chapter)
tasks.prompt: Listen to the final chapter of the audiobook while following along. Hearing the rhythm of Camus's prose can reveal nuances the silent reading misses. Note one sentence that landed differently when heard aloud.
tasks.output: One sentence noted as landing differently in audio.
checklist: Identified one sentence that resonated differently aloud.
Reflected briefly on why the sound changed the meaning.

tasks.title: Reading response 3: Must we imagine Sisyphus happy?
tasks.prompt: In approximately 300 words, answer: What does Camus mean by 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy'? Is this a descriptive claim, a prescriptive one, or something else? Is it convincing? End with your own view: can you imagine Sisyphus happy? Why or why not?
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Classified the type of claim (descriptive, prescriptive, other).
Engaged with whether the claim is convincing.
Stated your own position explicitly.
Word count is approximately 300 words.

weeklySchedule.topic: The Stranger: living the absurd

tasks.title: The Stranger, Part 1 (chapters 1-6)
tasks.prompt: Read Part 1 of The Stranger. Track Meursault's responses to key events: his mother's death, Marie's love, the offer of a Paris job, the killing on the beach. Note every moment where Meursault's reaction diverges from what 'normal' society expects. Mark at least three passages where the absurd is enacted rather than theorized.
tasks.output: Notes tracking Meursault's reactions, with three key passages marked.
checklist: Tracked Meursault's response to at least four key events.
Marked three passages where the absurd is enacted.
Noted the role of sun, heat, and physical sensation.

tasks.title: The Stranger, Part 2 (chapters 1-11, the trial and aftermath)
tasks.prompt: Read Part 2. The trial is the philosophical center: Meursault is judged not for killing a man but for not crying at his mother's funeral. Note how the prosecutor builds a case about Meursault's character, not his crime. In the final chapter, trace Meursault's confrontation with the chaplain and his breakthrough moment. Quote the passage where he embraces the 'benign indifference of the universe.'
tasks.output: Notes on the trial's logic and Meursault's final awakening, with two quotations.
checklist: Identified what Meursault is actually judged for.
Quoted the 'benign indifference' passage with page reference.
Noted the shift from passive to active absurd consciousness in the final chapter.

tasks.title: Reading response 4: Is Meursault an absurd hero?
tasks.prompt: In approximately 400 words, answer: Is Meursault an 'absurd hero' in the sense Camus describes in The Myth of Sisyphus? He does not articulate the absurd philosophically, but does he embody it? Consider whether his lack of emotional engagement is the same as the 'revolt, freedom, and passion' Camus prescribes. Argue for or against, using specific scenes from the novel.
tasks.output: ~400 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Defined what an absurd hero would look like per Sisyphus.
Compared Meursault to that definition using specific scenes.
Argued a clear position (for or against).
Word count is approximately 400 words.

weeklySchedule.topic: The Plague: from individual absurd to collective revolt

tasks.title: The Plague, Parts 1-3
tasks.prompt: Read Parts 1 through 3 of The Plague. Track the shift from individual life to collective crisis. Note how Rieux, Tarrou, and Rambert each respond to the plague differently. Identify the moment where Rambert chooses to stay despite having the chance to leave. What does this choice mean in Camus's framework? Mark three passages that connect to the concept of revolt.
tasks.output: Notes tracking three characters' responses, with three key passages marked.
checklist: Tracked Rieux, Tarrou, and Rambert's responses to the plague.
Identified Rambert's choice to stay and its significance.
Marked three passages connecting to revolt.
Noted the plague as metaphor (fascism, occupation, absurd itself).

tasks.title: The Plague, Parts 4-5
tasks.prompt: Read the final two parts. Note Tarrou's account of his life and his idea of becoming a 'saint without God.' Track the plague's retreat and Rieux's final reflection. In the closing pages, Rieux reveals he has been the narrator all along. Why? What does it mean to bear witness without heroism? Quote one passage about ordinary decency.
tasks.output: Notes on Tarrou's philosophy and Rieux's witness, with one key quotation.
checklist: Explained Tarrou's 'saint without God' concept.
Identified why Rieux reveals himself as narrator.
Quoted one passage about ordinary decency or witness.

tasks.title: Reading response 5: From Sisyphus to Rieux
tasks.prompt: In approximately 400 words, compare the individual revolt of Sisyphus with the collective revolt of Dr. Rieux. How does Camus's philosophy evolve from the solitary figure pushing a rock to a community fighting a plague? Is this a natural development or a contradiction? Use specific moments from both texts.
tasks.output: ~400 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Identified a specific moment from Sisyphus and one from The Plague.
Argued whether the shift is natural or contradictory.
Used textual evidence from both works.
Word count is approximately 400 words.

weeklySchedule.topic: Neither Victims nor Executioners, the Camus-Sartre split, and final paper

tasks.title: Neither Victims nor Executioners (full essay)
tasks.prompt: Read Camus's 1946 essay series. This is his most direct political statement: a rejection of both revolutionary violence and passive victimhood. Note his claim that 'what is needed today is not to solve all problems but to keep alive, through the apocalyptic vista, a modest thoughtfulness.' Identify his argument against the logic of history (the idea that violence today guarantees justice tomorrow). Mark three key passages.
tasks.output: Notes on Camus's political ethic, with three key passages marked.
checklist: Identified Camus's argument against the 'logic of history.'
Marked three key passages with section references.
Noted the connection to the Camus-Sartre split.

tasks.title: SEP entry on Camus (section on The Rebel and political philosophy)
tasks.prompt: Read the section of the SEP entry covering The Rebel and Camus's political thought. Focus on the Camus-Sartre split: what were the philosophical and political disagreements? Why did Camus reject Sartre's commitment to revolutionary violence? Take notes on the specific points of contention.
tasks.output: Notes on the Camus-Sartre split, listing at least three points of disagreement.
checklist: Listed at least three points of disagreement between Camus and Sartre.
Identified the role of The Rebel in the split.
Noted how this connects to Neither Victims nor Executioners.

tasks.title: Gregory Sadler lectures on Sisyphus (select 2-3 relevant lectures)
tasks.prompt: Browse the Sadler lecture index and watch 2-3 lectures most relevant to topics you found difficult across the course. Use these to solidify your understanding before writing the final paper. Note one insight that changed your reading.
tasks.output: One insight noted from the lectures.
checklist: Selected 2-3 lectures relevant to your weak points.
Noted one insight that changed your reading.

tasks.title: Final paper: Is Camus's philosophy livable?
tasks.prompt: Write a 1,000-1,200 word essay answering: Is Camus's response to the absurd, livable? Can a person genuinely live with revolt, freedom, and passion, without hope and without despair? Draw on at least three texts from the course (The Myth of Sisyphus, The Stranger, The Plague, and/or Neither Victims nor Executioners). Structure your essay: (1) define the absurd and Camus's prescribed response, (2) test it against one literary character (Meursault or Rieux), (3) test it against your own experience or a contemporary example, (4) argue for your conclusion. Include at least four textual quotations with proper attribution.
tasks.output: 1,000-1,200 word essay in your external workspace.
checklist: Defined the absurd and Camus's response in your own words.
Tested the philosophy against at least one literary character.
Connected to personal experience or a contemporary example.
Argued a clear conclusion.
Included at least four textual quotations with attribution.
Word count is between 1,000 and 1,200 words.
Proofread for structure, clarity, and grammar.

title: HUMN 201: Folklore, Mythology, and Comparative Mythology
subject: Humanities
description: A comparative study of folklore and mythology across world cultures. Read creation myths, hero tales, trickster narratives, and folktales from Greek, Norse, Mesopotamian, Indian, Celtic, Native American, African, and Mesoamerican traditions. Apply structural, functionalist, Jungian, and diffusionist theories to understand how myths shape and reflect the cultures that produce them.
objectives: Define myth, legend, folktale, and folklore, and distinguish among them using genre criteria from Bascom and Dundes.
Identify recurring motifs and narrative structures across world mythologies using the Aarne-Thompson-Uther and Stith Thompson motif indexes.

Apply major theoretical frameworks to myths, including functionalist (Malinowski), structuralist (Levi-Strauss), Jungian archetype (Campbell), ritualist (Frazer, Harrison), and morphological (Propp) approaches.
Compare creation myths, hero journeys, trickster narratives, and apocalypse myths from at least five distinct cultural traditions.
Analyze how myths encode social values, cosmological beliefs, and political structures within their source cultures.
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of the comparative method in cross-cultural mythology studies.
Construct an original comparative analysis of two myths from different traditions, supported by primary texts and secondary scholarship.

weeklySchedule.part: Foundations: Defining Myth, Legend, and Folktale
weeklySchedule.topic: What is mythology? Genre, definition, and the study of myth

tasks.title: Bascom, 'The Forms of Folklore: Prose Narratives' in Dundes, Sacred Narrative
tasks.prompt: Read Bascom's essay. Create a comparison table of myth, legend, and folktale using his three criteria: belief, setting in time/space, and principal characters. Identify one example of each genre from your own cultural background.
tasks.output: Comparison table with examples in your external workspace.
checklist: Are all three genres defined using Bascom's criteria?
Is at least one personal example given per genre?
Are the distinctions between genres clear and not overlapping?

tasks.title: Crash Course World Mythology #1: What Is Myth?
tasks.prompt: Watch episode 1. Note Mike Rugnetta's definition of myth as a story with 'significance and staying power.' Compare this to Bascom's more formal definition. Which do you find more useful for studying mythology?
tasks.output: One paragraph comparing the two definitions.
checklist: Is Rugnetta's definition accurately represented?
Is Bascom's definition accurately represented?
Is a preference stated with reasoning?

tasks.title: Eliade, The Sacred and the Profane, Ch. 1: Sacred Space and Making the World Sacred
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 1. Identify Eliade's concept of hierophany and explain how sacred space is constituted through myth. List three examples Eliade gives of sacred space construction.
tasks.output: Notes defining hierophany with three examples.
checklist: Is hierophany defined in your own words?
Are three specific examples from the text cited?
Is the connection between myth and sacred space explained?

tasks.title: Reading response 1: What counts as myth?
tasks.prompt: Write ~250 words. Using Bascom and Rugnetta, argue for or against the claim that 'myth' is a meaningful analytical category. Consider: if every culture defines its sacred narratives differently, can we use a single word for all of them?
tasks.output: ~250 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Are both Bascom and Rugnetta referenced?
Is a clear position taken?
Is one counterargument addressed?

weeklySchedule.part: Foundations: Defining Myth, Legend, and Folktale
weeklySchedule.topic: Theories of myth: Frazer, Malinowski, and the functionalist approach

tasks.title: Frazer, 'The Fall of Man' in Dundes, Sacred Narrative
tasks.prompt: Read Frazer's essay. Identify his comparative method: how does he trace the 'fall of man' motif across cultures? List three cultural traditions he connects. Note where his method crosses into speculative territory.
tasks.output: Notes listing three traditions and assessing Frazer's method.
checklist: Are three specific traditions identified from the text?
Is Frazer's comparative method described?
Is at least one speculative leap noted?

tasks.title: Malinowski, 'The Role of Myth in Life' in Dundes, Sacred Narrative
tasks.prompt: Read Malinowski's essay. Explain his functionalist claim that myth is not symbolic or allegorical but a 'living reality' that functions as a social charter. Compare this to Frazer's approach: where do they differ on what myth does?
tasks.output: Notes explaining functionalist theory and contrasting with Frazer.
checklist: Is the 'social charter' concept defined?
Is the contrast with Frazer explicit?
Is at least one Trobriand Island example referenced?

tasks.title: Crash Course World Mythology #12: Theories of Myth
tasks.prompt: Watch episode 12. Note the four theoretical approaches Rugnetta presents. Map each one to a theorist you have read so far (Frazer, Malinowski, Eliade). Which theory is missing from the episode that you think should be included?
tasks.output: Mapping table of theories to theorists with one gap identified.
checklist: Are at least four theories mapped?
Is each mapping justified with a reason?
Is one missing theory identified?

tasks.title: Reading response 2: Myth as living reality vs. myth as survival
tasks.prompt: Write ~250 words. Frazer treats myth as a 'survival' from an earlier stage of human thought. Malinowski treats myth as a living social institution. Which view better explains why myths persist in the modern world?
tasks.output: ~250 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Are both positions represented fairly?
Is the modern-world angle addressed?
Is a clear preference stated with reasoning?

weeklySchedule.part: Foundations: Defining Myth, Legend, and Folktale
weeklySchedule.topic: Structuralism: Propp's morphology and Levi-Strauss's binary oppositions

tasks.title: Propp, Morphology of the Folktale, Ch. II-III: The Method and Material / The Functions of Dramatis Personae
tasks.prompt: Read chapters II and III. List Propp's 31 functions. Pick any fairy tale you know (Cinderella, Jack and the Beanstalk, etc.) and map its plot to as many of Propp's functions as you can identify.
tasks.output: List of 31 functions plus a mapped fairy tale analysis.
checklist: Are all 31 functions listed?
Is a fairy tale mapped with specific function numbers?
Are missing functions noted rather than forced?

tasks.title: Levi-Strauss, 'The Story of Asdiwal' in Dundes, Sacred Narrative
tasks.prompt: Read Levi-Strauss's analysis of the Tsimshian myth of Asdiwal. Identify the binary oppositions he extracts (e.g., land/sea, upper/lower, endogamy/exogamy). Explain how his structural method differs from Propp's linear morphology.
tasks.output: Notes identifying binary oppositions and comparing methods.
checklist: Are at least three binary oppositions identified?
Is the paradigmatic vs. syntagmatic distinction explained?
Is the contrast with Propp explicit?

tasks.title: Reading response 3: Syntagmatic vs. paradigmatic analysis
tasks.prompt: Write ~300 words. Using Propp and Levi-Strauss, explain the difference between analyzing a narrative's chronological structure (syntagmatic) versus its underlying pattern of oppositions (paradigmatic). Apply both methods to a single myth or folktale of your choice.
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Are both methods defined?
Is a single narrative analyzed by both?
Do the two analyses yield different insights?

weeklySchedule.part: Creation Myths: Cosmogonies in Comparative Perspective
weeklySchedule.topic: Mesopotamian and Near Eastern creation myths: Enuma Elish and Genesis

tasks.title: Enuma Elish - The Babylonian Epic of Creation (full text)
tasks.prompt: Read the full Enuma Elish (Tablets I-VII). Outline the narrative: Apsu and Tiamat's primordial state, Marduk's birth and rise, the battle with Tiamat, and the creation of the world from her body. Note the political dimension: how does this myth justify Marduk's supremacy?
tasks.output: Narrative outline with political analysis.
checklist: Is the narrative arc complete (primordial state through creation)?
Is the political function of the myth identified?
Are specific tablet numbers referenced?

tasks.title: Crash Course World Mythology #2: Creation from the Void
tasks.prompt: Watch episode 2. Note the distinction between ex nihilo creation and creation from primordial matter. Place Enuma Elish and Genesis 1-3 on this spectrum. Which elements do the Babylonian and Hebrew creation narratives share, and which are distinctive?
tasks.output: Notes classifying both traditions with shared and distinctive elements.
checklist: Is the ex nihilo vs. primordial matter distinction applied?
Are at least three shared elements listed?
Are at least three distinctive elements listed?

tasks.title: Eliade, 'Cosmogonic Myth and Sacred History' in Dundes, Sacred Narrative
tasks.prompt: Read Eliade's essay. Explain his claim that every creation myth is also a paradigm for all subsequent creative acts. How does the cosmogony function as an 'archetype' for human activity? Give one example from Enuma Elish.
tasks.output: Notes explaining cosmogonic archetype with Enuma Elish example.
checklist: Is the archetype concept defined?
Is the Enuma Elish example specific?
Is the connection between creation and human activity explained?

tasks.title: Reading response 4: Creation myth as political charter
tasks.prompt: Write ~250 words. The Enuma Elish was recited at the Babylonian New Year festival (Akitu). Using Malinowski's functionalist framework, explain how this public performance of a creation myth functioned as a social and political charter for Babylonian society.
tasks.output: ~250 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Is Malinowski's framework applied?
Is the Akitu festival context included?
Is the political function specific rather than generic?

weeklySchedule.part: Creation Myths: Cosmogonies in Comparative Perspective
weeklySchedule.topic: Greek cosmogony: Hesiod's Theogony and the succession myth

tasks.title: Hesiod, Theogony (lines 1-1020, Evelyn-White translation)
tasks.prompt: Read the full Theogony. Map the succession of divine rulers: Ouranos to Kronos to Zeus. Identify the mechanisms of succession (castration, swallowing children, Titanomachy). Compare this to the Marduk-Tiamat conflict from Week 4.
tasks.output: Succession diagram with cross-cultural comparison to Enuma Elish.
checklist: Is the full succession chain (Ouranos-Kronos-Zeus) mapped?
Are the mechanisms of each transition specified?
Is the comparison to Enuma Elish explicit?

tasks.title: Crash Course World Mythology #4: Earth Mothers and Rebellious Sons
tasks.prompt: Watch episode 4. Note the pattern of generational conflict in creation myths (Gaia-Kronos-Zeus). List two other cultural traditions Rugnetta mentions that follow a similar pattern. How does this compare to the Norse succession (Ymir to Odin)?
tasks.output: Notes on generational conflict pattern with cross-cultural examples.
checklist: Are two non-Greek traditions identified?
Is the Norse comparison included?
Is the recurring pattern named and described?

tasks.title: Read Ashliman's folktexts: compare Greek and Mesopotamian succession myths
tasks.prompt: Browse Ashliman's folktexts collection for creation and succession narratives. Find at least two creation stories from non-Greek, non-Mesopotamian traditions (e.g., Norse, Egyptian, Indian). Note how they handle the question of primordial conflict vs. primordial harmony.
tasks.output: Notes on two additional creation traditions with conflict/harmony analysis.
checklist: Are two non-Greek, non-Mesopotamian traditions identified?
Is the conflict vs. harmony distinction applied?
Are specific story details cited?

tasks.title: Reading response 5: Why does the son overthrow the father?
tasks.prompt: Write ~300 words. The succession myth (father overthrown by son) appears in Greek, Mesopotamian, and Norse traditions. Using either Levi-Strauss's structuralism or Eliade's archetype theory, explain why this pattern recurs. What deeper structure or cosmic concern does it encode?
tasks.output: ~300 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Is a specific theoretical framework applied?
Are at least two cultural traditions referenced?
Is the structural or archetypal explanation clear?

weeklySchedule.part: Creation Myths: Cosmogonies in Comparative Perspective
weeklySchedule.topic: Norse cosmogony and eschatology: The Prose Edda, Voluspa, and Ragnarok

tasks.title: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning (The Fooling of Gylfe)
tasks.prompt: Read the Gylfaginning section of the Prose Edda. Map the Norse cosmogony: Ginnungagap, Ymir, Audhumla, Odin and his brothers, the creation of the world from Ymir's body. Then trace the eschatology: the signs of Ragnarok, the deaths of the gods, and the reborn world.
tasks.output: Cosmogony and eschatology map with key narrative beats.
checklist: Is the creation sequence (Ginnungagap through Ymir's body) mapped?
Is the Ragnarok sequence traced through key events?
Is the reborn world described?

tasks.title: Crash Course World Mythology #24: Ragnarok
tasks.prompt: Watch episode 24. Compare Rugnetta's presentation of Ragnarok with the Prose Edda account. Note where they differ in emphasis or detail. Is Ragnarok unique among world mythologies, or does it fit a broader apocalyptic pattern?
tasks.output: Notes comparing the two accounts with apocalyptic pattern analysis.
checklist: Are specific differences between the two accounts noted?
Is the question of uniqueness vs. pattern addressed?
Is at least one other apocalyptic tradition mentioned for comparison?

tasks.title: Crash Course World Mythology #23: The Apocalypse
tasks.prompt: Watch episode 23. List the apocalyptic traditions Rugnetta covers. Identify the recurring motifs: divine judgment, cosmic destruction, rebirth or renewal. Compare the Norse cyclic eschatology to the linear eschatology of the Book of Revelation.
tasks.output: Motif list with cyclic vs. linear eschatology comparison.
checklist: Are at least three apocalyptic traditions listed?
Are recurring motifs identified?
Is the cyclic vs. linear distinction applied to Norse and Christian traditions?

tasks.title: Reading response 6: Creation through destruction
tasks.prompt: Write ~250 words. Norse mythology is unusual in that the world is created from the body of a slain giant (Ymir) and ends with the deaths of the gods themselves (Ragnarok), followed by rebirth. Compare this to Enuma Elish, where the world is also made from a slain primordial being (Tiamat). What does the 'creation from violence' motif suggest about these cultures' views of order and chaos?
tasks.output: ~250 words in your external workspace.
checklist: Are both Norse and Mesopotamian traditions referenced?
Is the 'creation from violence' motif named?
Is a cultural interpretation of order vs. chaos offered?

weeklySchedule.topic: Campbell's Hero's Journey and the monomyth

tasks.title: Campbell, Hero with a Thousand Faces, Introduction and Part I (separation, initiation, return)
tasks.prompt: Read the introduction and Part I. Outline Campbell's 17-stage monomyth: the call to adventure, refusal of the call, supernatural aid, crossing the first threshold, belly of the whale, road of trials, meeting with the goddess, woman as temptress, atonement with the father, apotheosis, the ultimate boon, refusal of return, magic flight, rescue from without, crossing the return threshold, master of two worlds, freedom to live.
tasks.output: 17-stage outline with brief description of each stage.
checklist: Are all 17 stages listed with descriptions?
Is the three-act structure (separation, initiation, return) clear?

title: RELI 301: Comparative Religion Through the Work of Karen Armstrong
subject: Religion / Religious Studies
description: A 15-week intermediate course on comparative religion structured around the major works of Karen Armstrong, one of the world's foremost scholars of religion. Beginning with her memoir The Spiral Staircase and her Short History of Myth, the course moves through her comparative histories of the monotheistic traditions (A History of God, Islam, Holy War), her Axial Age study (The Great Transformation) and biography of the Buddha, her analyses of modernity and violence (The Battle for God, Fields of Blood), and her reflections on scripture, compassion, and nature (The Lost Art of Scripture, The Case for God, Twelve Steps to a Compassionate Life, Sacred Nature). Students write two comparative essays and a final research paper.
objectives: Trace Karen Armstrong's biographical journey and explain how her personal experience shapes her comparative method
Define and apply the distinction between mythos and logos as Armstrong frames it
Compare the development of monotheism across Judaism, Christianity, and Islam using Armstrong's historical framework
Explain the Axial Age concept and evaluate its usefulness as a comparative tool across Chinese, Indian, Greek, and Israelite traditions
Analyze Armstrong's argument that fundamentalism is a modern phenomenon rather than a return to premodern religion
Evaluate Armstrong's claim that religion is not the primary cause of violence and that the secular state has been more destructive
Distinguish premodern allegorical scriptural reading from modern literalism and explain why Armstrong considers literalism a distortion
Articulate Armstrong's vision of compassion as the essence of religion and assess it critically
Synthesize Armstrong's major themes into a coherent understanding of comparative religion as a discipline

title: HUMN 250: Storytelling Across Media
subject: Humanities
description: A cross-media exploration of narrative craft spanning oral tradition, literature, film, television, and interactive games. Students study the cognitive and evolutionary foundations of storytelling, examine how structure, character, and theme operate differently across media, and produce original narrative work in multiple forms. The course treats theory and practice as inseparable: every concept is applied through writing, analysis, and creative projects.
objectives: Analyze the cognitive, evolutionary, and cultural functions of storytelling across human history.
Identify and apply core narrative structures including three-act form, the hero's journey, and non-linear architectures.
Construct compelling characters with internal conflict, desire, and dimensional depth.
Compare how narrative techniques translate across oral, written, visual, and interactive media.
Evaluate the role of audience agency and participation in interactive storytelling forms.
Apply principles of pacing, tension, and dramatic irony to original narrative work.
Revise and polish a narrative portfolio demonstrating craft across at least two media forms.
Articulate a personal theory of story grounded in both classical theory and contemporary practice.

resources.label: The Science of Storytelling by Will Storr
resources.note: Primary textbook. Neuroscience and psychology of story craft, with practical 'Sacred Flaw Approach'. Widely used in creative writing programs.

resources.label: The Storytelling Animal by Jonathan Gottschall
resources.note: Evolutionary and cognitive theory of why humans tell stories. Author's official page with book details.

resources.label: Wired for Story by Lisa Cron
resources.note: Brain science approach to hooking readers. Published by Ten Speed Press. Author teaches at UCLA Extension and SVA.

resources.label: Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting by Robert McKee
resources.note: Comprehensive craft guide covering story design, act structure, scene craft, and genre. Applicable across page, stage, and screen. Author's official website.

resources.label: The Seven Basic Plots: Why We Tell Stories by Christopher Booker
resources.note: Jungian analysis of seven archetypal plot structures across literature, myth, and film. 736 pages, published by Bloomsbury Continuum.

resources.label: Pixar in a Box: The Art of Storytelling (Khan Academy)
resources.note: Free interactive course from Pixar and Khan Academy. Covers story structure, visual storytelling, character-driven narrative, pitching, and feedback.

resources.label: Brandon Sanderson BYU Creative Writing Lectures (2020)
resources.note: Full university course on writing craft: plot, setting, character, and business. Free on YouTube.

resources.label: Will Storr: Learn Storytelling in 72 Minutes (YouTube)
resources.note: Condensed overview of Storr's storytelling methodology. Good companion to the primary textbook.

resources.label: Folktales and Oral Storytelling: American Folklife Center Collections (Library of Congress)
resources.note: Research guide with audiovisual recordings, manuscripts, and resources on oral storytelling traditions including the National Storytelling Festival collection.

resources.label: Stories and Storytelling: Introduction to Narrative (Columbia University)
resources.note: Columbia ICLS course page. Examines storytelling across fiction, non-fiction, film, poetry, and autobiography. Useful for syllabus design reference.

weeklySchedule.topic: Character: the heart of narrative

tasks.title: Storr: The Science of Storytelling, chapters on character and the flawed self
tasks.prompt: Read the chapters on character and the 'Sacred Flaw'. Identify Storr's claim about how characters' flawed self-models drive story. Pick a character from any medium and identify their 'sacred flaw' using Storr's framework.
tasks.output: Notes on the Sacred Flaw framework plus one character analysis.
checklist: Defined the 'sacred flaw' in your own words.
Chose a specific character and named their flaw.
Explained how the flaw drives the story's conflict.

tasks.title: McKee: Story, Chapter 5 (Structure and Character)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 5. Identify McKee's argument about how character is revealed through choices under pressure. Write down the difference between 'characterization' (observable traits) and 'true character' (revealed through choice).
tasks.output: Notes on characterization vs true character with examples.
checklist: Distinguished characterization from true character.
Identified how pressure reveals character in McKee's view.
Noted at least one example McKee uses.

tasks.title: Cron: Wired for Story, Chapters 3-5 (on character and the brain)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapters 3-5. Identify Cron's claim about the 'neural story net' and how the brain fills gaps in character information. Note one way this connects to Storr's or McKee's framework.
tasks.output: Notes on the neural story net and its connection to other frameworks.
checklist: Defined the 'neural story net' in your own words.
Connected Cron's concept to Storr or McKee.
Noted one implication for your own writing.

tasks.title: Reading response 3: Character analysis across media
tasks.prompt: Choose one character that appears in at least two media (e.g., a book adapted to film, a game character with backstory lore). Write 400 words on how the character is revealed differently in each medium. What does each medium do well that the other cannot?
tasks.output: ~400 words comparing character revelation across two media.
checklist: Chose a character that appears in two media.
Analyzed how each medium reveals character differently.
Identified a medium-specific strength for each.
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Character profile
tasks.prompt: Choose one of your three premise seeds from Week 2. Develop the protagonist: write a one-paragraph backstory, identify their sacred flaw (Storr), their deepest desire, and the choice that would most reveal their true character (McKee).
tasks.output: A one-page character profile with flaw, desire, and revelatory choice.
checklist: Wrote a backstory paragraph.
Named the character's sacred flaw.
Identified the character's deepest desire.
Described a choice that reveals true character.

weeklySchedule.topic: World and setting: creating immersive story worlds

tasks.title: McKee: Story, Chapter 3 (Structure and Setting)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 3. Identify McKee's concepts of 'setting', 'genre', and 'world of the story'. Note how setting constrains and enables narrative possibilities. Pick a story world you admire and describe how its setting shapes its conflicts.
tasks.output: Notes on McKee's setting concepts with one world analysis.
checklist: Defined setting, genre, and world in McKee's terms.
Chose a story world and described its constraints.
Connected setting to conflict in your analysis.

tasks.title: Storr: The Science of Storytelling, chapter on 'Creating a World'
tasks.prompt: Read the 'Creating a World' section. Identify Storr's concept of 'change' as the engine of story worlds. Note how he connects worldbuilding to the brain's model-making process.
tasks.output: Notes on worldbuilding through the lens of cognitive model-making.
checklist: Defined Storr's concept of change in story worlds.
Connected worldbuilding to brain model-making.
Noted one example Storr uses.

tasks.title: Pixar in a Box: The Art of Storytelling (Unit 2)
tasks.prompt: Work through Pixar in a Box Unit 2 on storytelling. Note how Pixar approaches storyboarding, visual storytelling, and the iterative feedback process. Write down one technique you could apply to your own work.
tasks.output: Notes on Pixar's storytelling pipeline and one applicable technique.
checklist: Described Pixar's storyboarding process.
Noted the role of pitching and feedback.
Identified one technique to apply to your work.

tasks.title: Reading response 4: The world as character
tasks.prompt: Choose a story world (from film, literature, or games) where the setting functions as a character in its own right. Write 400 words on how the world creates pressure, constrains choices, and drives conflict. Reference McKee and/or Storr.
tasks.output: ~400 words on setting as a narrative force.
checklist: Chose a world where setting drives narrative.
Analyzed how the world creates pressure and constrains choice.
Referenced McKee or Storr by name.
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Portfolio: World sketch for your story
tasks.prompt: Using the character you developed in Week 3, sketch the story world they inhabit. Write a one-page world bible covering: the core conflict of the world, three rules or constraints, and one scene where the world forces your character into a difficult choice.
tasks.output: A one-page world bible with conflict, rules, and a scene sketch.
checklist: Defined the world's core conflict.
Listed three rules or constraints.
Wrote one scene where the world pressures the character.

weeklySchedule.topic: Oral storytelling: the ancient art

tasks.title: Library of Congress: Folktales and Oral Storytelling guide
tasks.prompt: Browse the American Folklife Center guide on folktales and oral storytelling. Read the Introduction and explore at least two sections (e.g., Jack Tales, Trickster Tales, the International Storytelling Collection). Note how oral traditions differ from written ones in structure, repetition, and audience interaction.
tasks.output: Notes on oral vs written storytelling differences with two examples.
checklist: Read the introduction and two sections of the guide.
Identified three differences between oral and written storytelling.
Named at least two specific storytelling traditions.

tasks.title: Gottschall: The Storytelling Animal, chapters on oral tradition and story in pre-literate cultures
tasks.prompt: Read the chapters on oral storytelling and pre-literate narrative. Identify Gottschall's claims about how oral traditions shape memory, community, and cultural transmission. Note one way these findings challenge assumptions about 'primitive' storytelling.
tasks.output: Notes on oral tradition's cognitive and social functions.
checklist: Identified two functions of oral storytelling from Gottschall.
Noted one way oral tradition challenges modern assumptions.
Connected findings to your own experience of spoken stories.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture: Plot part 2 and setting lectures
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's lectures on plot and setting. Note how his approach to narrative structure applies to written fiction specifically. Consider how oral storytelling principles (repetition, audience response) might translate to written craft.
tasks.output: Notes connecting Sanderson's craft to oral storytelling principles.
checklist: Noted Sanderson's key plot and setting principles.
Identified one connection to oral storytelling.
Wrote one question about cross-media translation.

tasks.title: Reading response 5: The listener's story
tasks.prompt: Write 400 words on the fundamental differences between a story told orally and one written down. Consider: repetition, audience feedback, memory, variation, and presence. Use at least one example from the Library of Congress or Gottschall readings.
tasks.output: ~400 words comparing oral and written narrative.
checklist: Identified at least three structural differences.
Used a specific example from the readings.
Considered audience dynamics.
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Practice: Tell a story aloud
tasks.prompt: Choose a folk tale or personal anecdote. Tell it aloud to someone (or record yourself) without reading from a text. Then transcribe what you actually said. Compare the told version to what you 'meant' to say. Note what changed in the telling.
tasks.output: An audio recording or live telling, plus a transcription with notes on variation.
checklist: Told the story aloud without reading.
Transcribed the actual telling.
Noted at least three differences from the intended version.
Reflected on what the oral medium added or changed.

weeklySchedule.topic: Written narrative: from short stories to novels

tasks.title: Cron: Wired for Story, Chapters 6-9 (on the written page and the reader's brain)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapters 6-9. Identify Cron's claims about how the brain processes written narrative differently from other forms. Note her concept of 'the story net' and how writers can exploit gaps in reader knowledge.
tasks.output: Notes on written narrative's cognitive mechanisms.
checklist: Identified how the brain processes written narrative.
Defined Cron's 'story net'.
Noted one technique for exploiting reader knowledge gaps.

tasks.title: Storr: The Science of Storytelling, chapter on plot and structure in written narrative
tasks.prompt: Read the chapters on plot structure and the Sacred Flaw Approach's application to prose. Note how Storr's framework applies specifically to written fiction. Write down one way his approach differs from McKee's screenwriting focus.
tasks.output: Notes on Storr's prose-specific applications and comparison to McKee.
checklist: Identified one prose-specific application of Storr's framework.
Compared Storr's approach to McKee's.
Noted a practical technique from the chapter.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture: Character lectures
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's character lectures from the BYU series. Note his approach to character arcs in prose fiction specifically. Write down one technique for creating character sympathy that you haven't encountered in McKee or Storr.
tasks.output: Notes on Sanderson's character craft and one new technique.
checklist: Identified Sanderson's approach to character arcs.
Found one technique not covered by McKee or Storr.
Noted how prose enables character interiority.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Draft a short story opening (1000 words)
tasks.prompt: Using the character and world from Weeks 3-4, write the opening 1000 words of a short story. Establish the protagonist's sacred flaw, the world's core conflict, and an inciting incident. Apply at least one technique from Cron (exploit a knowledge gap) and one from Storr (the Sacred Flaw).
tasks.output: A 1000-word short story opening.
checklist: Established the protagonist's flaw within the first 500 words.
Introduced the world's core conflict.
Included an inciting incident.
Applied one Cron technique and one Storr technique.
Word count is approximately 1000 (900-1100).

tasks.title: Reading response 6: The interiority advantage
tasks.prompt: Write 300 words on what written narrative can do that no other medium can. Focus on interiority, the reader's co-creation of the story world, and the absence of a time constraint. Reference Cron or Storr.
tasks.output: ~300 words on the unique properties of written narrative.
checklist: Identified at least two unique properties of written narrative.
Referenced Cron or Storr by name.
Stayed within 250-350 words.

weeklySchedule.topic: Film and visual storytelling

tasks.title: McKee: Story, Part 3 (Principles of Story Design, Chapters 7-9)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapters 7-9 on the inciting incident, act design, and scene design. Note how McKee's framework applies specifically to screen storytelling. Identify the 'inciting incident' in one film you know and trace how it sets the story in motion.
tasks.output: Notes on McKee's story design principles with a film analysis.
checklist: Defined inciting incident, act design, and scene design.
Traced the inciting incident in a specific film.
Connected McKee's screen-specific tools to earlier readings.

tasks.title: Pixar in a Box: Visual storytelling and cinematography modules
tasks.prompt: Work through the Pixar in a Box modules on visual storytelling. Note how camera, staging, and editing choices convey story information without dialogue. Write down one principle of visual storytelling you can apply to your own work.
tasks.output: Notes on visual storytelling principles with one applicable takeaway.
checklist: Identified three visual storytelling techniques.
Noted one principle applicable to your own work.
Considered how visual storytelling differs from prose.

tasks.title: Storr: The Science of Storytelling, film examples and the 'dramatic question'
tasks.prompt: Read the section on the 'Dramatic Question'. Identify how Storr applies his framework to film examples (he uses Breaking Bad, Harry Potter, and others). Note how the dramatic question differs from McKee's inciting incident.
tasks.output: Notes on the dramatic question and its relation to McKee's framework.
checklist: Defined the dramatic question in your own words.
Distinguished it from McKee's inciting incident.
Applied it to one film example.

tasks.title: Reading response 7: Show, don't tell, revisited
tasks.prompt: Write 400 words on how film solves the 'show don't tell' problem that written narrative wrestles with. Consider: what does film sacrifice by showing? What does it gain? Use a specific film scene as your example. Reference McKee or Storr.
tasks.output: ~400 words on film's visual storytelling tradeoffs.
checklist: Analyzed a specific film scene.
Identified what film gains and loses by showing.
Referenced McKee or Storr by name.
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Script a scene (2-3 pages)
tasks.prompt: Take the story opening you wrote in Week 6 and adapt it into a 2-3 page screenplay scene. Focus on what can be shown visually vs what must be cut or conveyed through action. Apply McKee's scene design principles.
tasks.output: A 2-3 page screenplay scene adaptation.
checklist: Adapted the Week 6 story opening into screenplay format.
Used visual storytelling instead of interior monologue.
Applied McKee's scene design (turning point, behavior change).
Length is 2-3 pages.

weeklySchedule.topic: Television and long-form narrative

tasks.title: McKee: Story, relevant sections on long-form structure and act design (Chapters 9-10)
tasks.prompt: Read the chapters on act design and scene design. Consider how McKee's three-act film structure extends or breaks down in a multi-season television series. Write down how a TV season might use McKee's act structure at two levels: the episode and the season.
tasks.output: Notes on multi-level act structure in TV.
checklist: Identified how act structure works at episode and season level.
Noted where McKee's film framework strains in long-form.
Considered a specific TV show as example.

tasks.title: Storr: The Science of Storytelling, sections on serialized and long-form examples
tasks.prompt: Review Storr's examples drawn from Breaking Bad and other serialized TV. Note how the 'Sacred Flaw' operates over many hours of story rather than two. Consider how long-form changes the audience's relationship to the flaw.
tasks.output: Notes on the Sacred Flaw in serialized narrative.
checklist: Identified how the Sacred Flaw evolves over a season.
Noted the difference between film and TV flaw escalation.
Considered audience relationship to long-form character flaws.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture: Business of writing and long-form series structure
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's lecture on series structure and the business of writing. Note his approach to multi-book arcs, foreshadowing, and managing reader expectations over long series. Write one principle you'd apply to a serialized story.
tasks.output: Notes on series structure and one applicable principle.
checklist: Noted Sanderson's approach to multi-book arcs.
Identified a foreshadowing technique.
Wrote one principle for serialized storytelling.

tasks.title: Reading response 8: The long-form flaw
tasks.prompt: Choose a TV series you know well (at least 2 seasons). Write 400 words on how the protagonist's flaw evolves across seasons. Does the series 'solve' the flaw, or does it deepen? Reference Storr's Sacred Flaw framework.
tasks.output: ~400 words on flaw evolution in a TV series.
checklist: Named a specific series and protagonist.
Traced the flaw across at least two seasons.
Referenced Storr's Sacred Flaw framework.
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Series pitch (one page)
tasks.prompt: Write a one-page pitch for a TV series based on your story concept. Include: the logline, the protagonist's flaw, the season one arc, and how the flaw could evolve over three seasons. This exercises long-form thinking on your portfolio concept.
tasks.output: A one-page TV series pitch with multi-season flaw arc.
checklist: Wrote a logline (1-2 sentences).
Defined the protagonist's flaw.
Outlined a season one arc.
Sketched a three-season flaw evolution.

weeklySchedule.topic: Games and interactive storytelling

tasks.title: Cron: Wired for Story, re-read Chapter 1 with interactive narrative in mind
tasks.prompt: Re-read Cron's Chapter 1 with a new question: what happens to the brain's story net when the audience is also the protagonist? Note how Cron's framework for hooking readers might apply to player motivation. Write down one way agency changes the cognitive experience of story.
tasks.output: Notes on agency and the reader/player's cognitive experience.
checklist: Noted how agency changes the story net's operation.
Identified one way player motivation differs from reader motivation.
Connected Cron's framework to game design.

tasks.title: McKee: Story, Chapter 4 (Structure and Genre) applied to games
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 4 on genre. Consider how McKee's genre constraints apply to games. Do game genres (RPG, adventure, simulation) impose different narrative structures than film genres? Write down two genre constraints specific to games.
tasks.output: Notes on game-specific genre constraints.
checklist: Identified two game-specific genre constraints.
Compared game genre to film genre constraints.
Noted how genre shapes narrative possibilities in games.

tasks.title: Pixar in a Box: Character and feedback modules (for interactive comparison)
tasks.prompt: Work through the Pixar in a Box modules on character and feedback. Consider how the iterative feedback process at Pixar parallels game playtesting. Note one principle from Pixar's process that game narrative designers could adopt.
tasks.output: Notes connecting Pixar's feedback loop to game playtesting.
checklist: Described Pixar's iterative feedback process.
Connected it to game playtesting.
Identified one cross-applicable principle.

tasks.title: Reading response 9: The problem of agency
tasks.prompt: Write 400 words on the central tension of interactive storytelling: the author wants to control the story's meaning, but the player wants agency. How do games resolve (or fail to resolve) this tension? Use a specific game as your example. Reference at least one framework from the course.
tasks.output: ~400 words on the authorship vs agency tension in games.
checklist: Defined the authorship vs agency tension.
Used a specific game as example.
Referenced at least one course framework (McKee, Cron, Storr).
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Interactive narrative outline
tasks.prompt: Design an outline for an interactive narrative version of your story concept. Include: the core dramatic question, three branching decision points, the consequences of each branch, and how the protagonist's flaw is tested differently depending on player choices. Map this onto one page.
tasks.output: A one-page interactive narrative outline with branching structure.
checklist: Stated the core dramatic question.
Designed three branching decision points.
Described consequences for each branch.
Showed how the flaw is tested differently per branch.

weeklySchedule.topic: Transmedia and cross-medium storytelling

tasks.title: Booker: The Seven Basic Plots, sections on modern and cross-medium storytelling
tasks.prompt: Read Booker's later chapters on how storytelling has changed in the modern era, including his argument about stories 'losing the plot'. Consider how transmedia storytelling, where a single story world spans multiple media, fits or challenges Booker's archetypal framework. Write down one way transmedia complicates the seven-plot model.
tasks.output: Notes on how transmedia challenges Booker's model.
checklist: Summarized Booker's argument about modern storytelling.
Identified one way transmedia complicates the seven-plot model.
Considered whether archetypes survive across media.

tasks.title: Storr: The Science of Storytelling, cross-medium examples (Harry Potter, Breaking Bad, Greek drama)
tasks.prompt: Review Storr's examples that span media (Harry Potter across books and films, Greek drama across oral and written traditions). Note how the Sacred Flaw survives translation across media. Write down what stays constant and what changes when a story moves from one medium to another.
tasks.output: Notes on what is constant vs what changes in cross-medium translation.
checklist: Identified what stays constant across media (the flaw, the dramatic question).
Identified what changes (pacing, interiority, agency).
Used at least one of Storr's cross-media examples.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture: Adaptation and cross-medium writing
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's lectures covering adaptation and cross-media storytelling from his BYU series. Note his practical advice for writers working across media. Write down one principle for preserving story integrity when adapting between forms.
tasks.output: Notes on adaptation principles from Sanderson.
checklist: Noted Sanderson's adaptation advice.
Identified one principle for preserving story integrity.
Considered a specific adaptation example.

tasks.title: Reading response 10: What survives the medium change?
tasks.prompt: Write 400 words on what is essential to a story and what is medium-specific. When a story moves from book to film to game, what must survive and what must be reinvented? Use a specific transmedia property as your example. Reference at least two course authors.
tasks.output: ~400 words on transmedia story essentials.
checklist: Distinguished essential story elements from medium-specific ones.
Used a specific transmedia property as example.
Referenced at least two course authors.
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Midterm essay: A theory of story across media (1500 words)
tasks.prompt: Write a 1500-word midterm essay synthesizing your understanding of storytelling across media. Your thesis should answer: What is essential to storytelling, and how do different media reshape that essence? Draw on at least four course authors (Storr, Gottschall, Cron, McKee, Booker) and at least two media forms. This is the capstone of Part 2.
tasks.output: ~1500 word midterm essay.
checklist: Stated a clear thesis about storytelling across media.
Cited at least four course authors.
Discussed at least two media forms.
Included specific examples from readings and viewings.
Word count is approximately 1500 (1400-1600).

weeklySchedule.topic: Theme, meaning, and the controlling idea

tasks.title: McKee: Story, Chapter 6 (Structure and Meaning)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 6. Identify McKee's concepts of 'controlling idea' and 'counter-idea'. Note how theme emerges through structure rather than being imposed on it. Choose a story you know and identify its controlling idea and counter-idea.
tasks.output: Notes on controlling idea with a story analysis.
checklist: Defined controlling idea and counter-idea.
Applied them to a specific story.
Noted how theme emerges from structure.

tasks.title: Storr: The Science of Storytelling, chapter on 'Plot, Endings, and Meaning'
tasks.prompt: Read the section on endings and meaning. Identify how Storr connects the Sacred Flaw to the story's thematic resolution. Note the difference between a story that 'earns' its ending and one that does not.
tasks.output: Notes on the connection between flaw and thematic resolution.
checklist: Connected the Sacred Flaw to thematic resolution.
Defined what it means for a story to 'earn' its ending.
Noted one example from Storr.

tasks.title: Booker: The Seven Basic Plots, sections on the deeper meaning of archetypes
tasks.prompt: Read Booker's sections on the psychological and spiritual significance of the seven plots. Note his Jungian claim that plots reflect psychic patterns. Write down one way Booker's archetypal approach to theme differs from McKee's structural approach.
tasks.output: Notes comparing archetypal and structural approaches to theme.
checklist: Summarized Booker's Jungian approach to theme.
Compared it to McKee's structural approach.
Identified which approach you find more useful and why.

tasks.title: Reading response 11: Whose theme is it?
tasks.prompt: Write 400 words on the tension between authorial intent and reader interpretation in theme. Can a story mean something its author did not intend? Use McKee's controlling idea and Storr's Sacred Flaw to structure your argument. Use a specific story as example.
tasks.output: ~400 words on theme and interpretation.
checklist: Addressed the intent vs interpretation question.
Used McKee and/or Storr to structure the argument.
Used a specific story as example.
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Identify your story's controlling idea
tasks.prompt: Return to your portfolio story concept. Write one sentence stating the controlling idea (what the story argues is true about life) and one sentence stating the counter-idea. Then note how your protagonist's flaw dramatizes this tension.
tasks.output: Controlling idea, counter-idea, and flaw connection for your portfolio story.
checklist: Wrote a clear controlling idea sentence.
Wrote a clear counter-idea sentence.
Connected the flaw to the thematic tension.

weeklySchedule.topic: Dialogue and voice

tasks.title: McKee: Story, Chapter 18 (The Text) and sections on dialogue
tasks.prompt: Read Chapter 18 and any sections on dialogue. Identify McKee's principles for effective dialogue: subtext, economy, and the gap between what characters say and what they mean. Note his distinction between 'text' and 'subtext'.
tasks.output: Notes on McKee's dialogue principles with subtext examples.
checklist: Defined text vs subtext.
Identified three dialogue principles from McKee.
Noted one example of subtext from a story you know.

tasks.title: Cron: Wired for Story, chapters on voice and the reader's engagement
tasks.prompt: Read the chapters on voice and engagement. Identify Cron's claims about how the brain responds to voice and narrative tone. Note one way a strong narrative voice exploits the brain's story net.
tasks.output: Notes on voice and the brain's response to narrative tone.
checklist: Identified how the brain responds to narrative voice.
Connected voice to the story net concept.
Noted one practical takeaway for your own writing.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture: Dialogue and prose craft
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's lecture on dialogue. Note his practical techniques for writing distinct character voices. Write down one technique for making each character sound different that you haven't encountered in McKee or Cron.
tasks.output: Notes on Sanderson's dialogue craft and one new technique.
checklist: Noted Sanderson's dialogue techniques.
Found one technique not covered by McKee or Cron.
Considered how dialogue differs across media (prose vs script).

tasks.title: Reading response 12: The gap between said and meant
tasks.prompt: Write 350 words on a scene from any medium where the subtext (what is meant) contradicts the text (what is said). Analyze how the gap creates dramatic tension. Reference McKee's subtext concept.
tasks.output: ~350 words on subtext in a specific scene.
checklist: Chose a scene with clear text/subtext gap.
Analyzed how the gap creates tension.
Referenced McKee's subtext concept.
Stayed within 300-400 words.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Write a dialogue scene
tasks.prompt: Write a 500-word dialogue scene between your protagonist and one other character from your portfolio concept. The scene must contain clear subtext: the characters are talking about one thing on the surface but the real conflict is about something else. Apply McKee's subtext principles and one technique from Sanderson.
tasks.output: A 500-word dialogue scene with subtext.
checklist: Surface conversation differs from the real conflict.
Applied McKee's subtext principles.
Applied one technique from Sanderson.
Each character has a distinct voice.
Word count is approximately 500 (450-550).

weeklySchedule.topic: Pacing, tension, and audience engagement

tasks.title: McKee: Story, Chapters 10-11 (Scene Design and Scene Analysis)
tasks.prompt: Read Chapters 10-11 on scene design and analysis. Identify McKee's concept of the 'turning point' and how scenes must 'turn'. Note how pacing is controlled at the scene level through the rhythm of expectation and surprise. Apply the 'beat' concept to one scene from a story you know.
tasks.output: Notes on scene turning points and pacing with one scene analysis.
checklist: Defined the turning point in McKee's terms.
Noted how pacing works at the scene level.
Applied the beat concept to a specific scene.

tasks.title: Cron: Wired for Story, chapters on tension and the dopamine loop
tasks.prompt: Read Cron's chapters on how the brain's dopamine system drives narrative engagement. Identify her claim about how curiosity gaps sustain attention. Note one technique for creating a curiosity gap in your own writing.
tasks.output: Notes on the dopamine loop and curiosity gaps.
checklist: Defined the curiosity gap in Cron's terms.
Connected dopamine to narrative engagement.
Noted one technique for creating curiosity gaps.

tasks.title: Storr: The Science of Storytelling, chapter on 'moments of change' and pacing
tasks.prompt: Read Storr's section on 'moments of change'. Identify how he connects pacing to the brain's change-detection system. Note how this differs from McKee's structural approach to pacing.
tasks.output: Notes on Storr's cognitive approach to pacing.
checklist: Defined 'moments of change' in Storr's terms.
Connected change-detection to pacing.
Compared cognitive and structural approaches to pacing.

tasks.title: Reading response 13: How does your medium control time?
tasks.prompt: Write 400 words on how pacing differs across at least two media. How does a book control pacing differently from a film? How does a game? Use Cron's curiosity gap and McKee's turning points to structure your analysis. Use a specific example for each medium.
tasks.output: ~400 words on medium-specific pacing.
checklist: Compared pacing across at least two media.
Referenced Cron and McKee.
Used a specific example for each medium.
Stayed within 350-450 words.

tasks.title: Practice: Rewrite a scene at two different paces
tasks.prompt: Take the dialogue scene from Week 12. Rewrite it twice: once at a slow, contemplative pace and once at a fast, urgent pace. Keep the same subtext but change sentence length, paragraph breaks, and information density. Write a short note on which version works better and why.
tasks.output: Two versions of the Week 12 scene at different paces, plus a note.
checklist: Rewrote the scene at a slow pace.
Rewrote the scene at a fast pace.
Changed sentence length and information density between versions.
Wrote a note on which version works better and why.

weeklySchedule.topic: The revision process: from draft to final

tasks.title: McKee: Story, Part 4 (The Writer at Work, Chapters 17-19)
tasks.prompt: Read Part 4, McKee's chapters on the writer at work. Identify his approach to revision: the 'writer's method', dealing with problems, and the discipline of rewriting. Note one revision strategy you can apply to your portfolio.
tasks.output: Notes on McKee's revision method and one applicable strategy.
checklist: Summarized McKee's writer's method.
Identified one revision strategy for your portfolio.
Noted how McKee frames problems and solutions.

tasks.title: Cron: Wired for Story, chapters on revision and the story blueprint
tasks.prompt: Read Cron's chapters on revision and the 'story blueprint' approach. Identify her claim that revision is about fixing the story's underlying logic, not polishing prose. Note how her brain-based approach to revision differs from McKee's.
tasks.output: Notes on Cron's revision approach and comparison to McKee.
checklist: Defined Cron's 'story blueprint' concept.
Compared brain-based and structural revision approaches.
Noted one revision principle from Cron.

tasks.title: Sanderson Lecture: Revision and the writing process
tasks.prompt: Watch Sanderson's lecture on revision and the writing process. Note his practical revision workflow. Write down one concrete revision technique Sanderson uses that differs from McKee or Cron.
tasks.output: Notes on Sanderson's revision workflow and one new technique.
checklist: Described Sanderson's revision workflow.
Found one technique that differs from McKee or Cron.
Noted a practical step you can apply this week.

tasks.title: Reading response 14: What is revision, really?
tasks.prompt: Write 350 words on the difference between revising (rethinking the story's logic) and editing (polishing the prose). Use McKee, Cron, and Sanderson to define what revision truly means. Which of the three approaches to revision do you find most useful for your own work?
tasks.output: ~350 words on revision vs editing.
checklist: Distinguished revision from editing.
Referenced McKee, Cron, and Sanderson.
Stated which approach is most useful for your work.
Stayed within 300-400 words.

tasks.title: Portfolio: Revise your short story opening
